result.plan_implied_asker: A fundamental long/short shop with an alt-data panel team that wants a causally defensible read on a specific competitive-substitution story to size a named position, not a cross-sectional signal desk
result.what_would_falsify: A rejected pre-trend joint F-test (β₋₆..β₋₂ not flat), a partial-identification breakdown value M close to the plan's own disqualifying bound (M≈0.5, i.e. a plausible pre-existing trend alone explains the post-period gap), or placebo channels (grocery/fuel/e-commerce spend, pseudo-adoption six months earlier, first-transaction-at-an-unrelated-merchant, the FanDuel-only pipeline) showing a comparable 'effect' — any of these is pre-committed as grounds to treat the substitution claim as not established.

issues.summary: The plan never states what the market (sell-side notes, DraftKings' own earnings-call commentary on prediction markets) already believes about Kalshi cannibalization, so a clean causal result may only confirm a thesis that is already in the multiple.
issues.why_it_applies_here: DraftKings management and sell-side analysts have already publicly discussed event-contract competition; the panel gives a genuine measurement edge (magnitude and timing ahead of reported financials), but the plan doesn't say whether the magnitude it expects to find is larger or smaller than what's implicitly priced, which is the difference between an investable finding and a well-executed confirmation of consensus.
issues.what_breaks: The PM step where the finding is translated into a position-size change: a statistically airtight β with no view on what was already assumed by the market gives no basis for sizing up or down.
issues.fix: Add one paragraph benchmarking the expected/found effect size against what sell-side models or DraftKings' own disclosed guidance already imply for prediction-market drag, so the causal estimate can be read as incremental or not.

issues.summary: DraftKings 'wallet share' (a secondary/cross-check outcome) falls mechanically once Kalshi dollars enter the denominator of total wallet, independent of any true reduction in DraftKings spend.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The moment a user has any Kalshi debit, total wallet = DraftKings + Kalshi + other by construction, so wallet share for that user-month declines even if DraftKings dollars are literally unchanged; this is the definitional-relationship failure mode, not a substitution measurement.
issues.what_breaks: If the primary dollars/retention estimates come back weak or ambiguous, the wallet-share cross-check could be read as corroborating substitution when it is guaranteed to move in that direction by definition.
issues.fix: Either drop wallet-share as corroborating evidence or restate it as a share of DraftKings-plus-other-sportsbook spend only (excluding Kalshi from the denominator), so it isn't tautologically responsive to adoption.

issues.summary: Because retail-scale event-contract sports trading on Kalshi only recently expanded, the adopter cohort studied is necessarily an early, possibly unrepresentative slice, while the fund's decision horizon (6-18 months) spans a period where adoption composition will likely broaden.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The robustness list itself flags dropping Nov 2024/Jan 2025 cohorts, which signals that a meaningful share of usable post-period data sits right at the recency edge — the population available to study is disproportionately the earliest, most engaged adopters, not the mainstream user the DraftKings thesis over the next 6-18 months depends on.
issues.what_breaks: External validity of the estimated β for sizing a position meant to hold over the next 6-18 months, if early adopters substitute more (or less) aggressively than the broader base that will follow.
issues.fix: Report the effect separately by adoption-cohort vintage (early vs. later within the sample) to see whether the estimated substitution is stable or an early-adopter artifact before extrapolating it forward.

issues.summary: The event-time window is fixed at -6..+6 months, so the study can speak to the lower end of the fund's 6-18 month horizon but says nothing about whether substitution persists, fades, or grows over the back half of that horizon.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Position sizing decisions on DraftKings implicitly bet on a directional trend holding for up to 18 months, but the design as specified stops observing three months short of that, and doesn't state a plan to re-run or extend the window as more post-period months accrue.
issues.what_breaks: A PM sizing a multi-quarter short/underweight based on a 6-month substitution estimate has no evidence on whether the effect is durable or a novelty-driven transient that reverses by month 12.
issues.fix: Pre-commit to a follow-up re-estimation at +12 (and ideally +18) once enough cohorts have matured, rather than treating the +6 window as the final answer.

result.overall: This is a well-built plan: the taxonomy, matching, event-study design, placebos, pre-trend and partial-identification checks, and explicit pre-commitment give the PM exactly the falsification handles the brief asks for, and the scope matches what a data team plus one engineer can actually run without new infrastructure. The remaining gaps are secondary polish, not structural — tie the finding back to what's already priced/discussed about Kalshi-DraftKings substitution, stop treating wallet share as independent corroborating evidence given its mechanical construction, check whether the studied adopters are representative of the wave still to come, and plan to extend the observation window toward the 18-month end of the fund's horizon.

result.plan_implied_asker: An applied-micro/causal-inference research team with dedicated econometric staff and infrastructure to build and maintain IV, GMM and matching pipelines — not a PM-facing fundamental shop; the plan assumes an audience that can evaluate Kleibergen-Paap statistics and Arellano-Bond bias on its own terms.
result.what_would_falsify: H1 is dead if β is statistically indistinguishable from the permuted/mechanical null at 5%, if the event-study ATT diverges from β×mean Δshare by more than ~2x (event study wins), if the six pre-trend leads are jointly significant (p ≤ 0.10), or if placebo categories (grocery/streaming/non-legal states/neobank fake-treatment) show effects comparable to the DK result.

issues.summary: The causal-inference stack (holdout-fit IV with Kleibergen-Paap, Arellano-Bond GMM, Callaway-Sant'Anna event study, wild cluster bootstrap) requires econometric specialization the stated 3-person data team and single engineer do not have and cannot maintain.
issues.why_it_applies_here: This exact team profile (a licensing/cleaning data team plus one engineer, no dedicated econometrician) is given in the brief, and the ultimate consumer is a PM who will ask 'what would have to be true for this to be wrong' in plain terms — a question this stack cannot be answered for without trusting the analyst's black box.
issues.what_breaks: Build risk on the estimation pipeline itself, and downstream, the PM cannot independently interrogate an F-stat or a GMM instrument set, so the sizing decision rests on trust rather than the PM's own judgment.
issues.fix: Make the fixed-effects regression with the permutation null and the event-study cross-check the primary deliverable — both produce PM-checkable outputs (wallet-accounting sum-to-100%, headline $ displaced) — and demote IV/Arellano-Bond to optional robustness only if the primary result is contested, always shown alongside the plain estimate.

issues.summary: The power/MDE calculation, explicitly labeled 'power first,' is textually the last item in Validation rather than the gate that determines whether the rest of the build is worth doing.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The clean adopter count here is bounded further by the broker-distributed Kalshi attribution gap (Robinhood/Webull), so the effective N for the cannibalization test could be small; whether the panel can even detect an economically relevant $ displacement is knowable cheaply and should precede the descriptor audits and multi-model build, not follow them in the document.
issues.what_breaks: Analyst time is sunk into hand-audited descriptor dictionaries, attribution-gap quantification, and multiple model specifications before learning whether the sample supports inference at a size that would move a position.
issues.fix: Run the MDE calculation off raw adopter counts and rough deposit variance before any audit or model-building step; treat a failing MDE as an immediate stop.

issues.summary: The plan never states how a well-identified per-user $-displaced-per-10-points-share estimate gets scaled into DKNG's (and Flutter/FD's) consolidated revenue or margin impact — the number that actually changes position sizing.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The stated deliverable of this work is to change sizing on named companies; a micro coefficient is silent on what share of DK's active base is affected, what share of DK revenue those users represent, and how fast it flows to reported financials — without that bridge the rigorously identified result cannot yet inform a position.
issues.what_breaks: The PM receives a clean causal estimate but still has to guess the firm-level magnitude, reintroducing the kind of unsupported extrapolation the rest of the plan is careful to avoid.
issues.fix: Add an explicit, separately-flagged aggregation step using adopter penetration, the H4 tenure/spend-decile weights, and coverage-adjusted extrapolation to DK's reported base, presented as a range — or state plainly that this study answers the mechanism question only and a follow-on step is required for sizing.

issues.summary: The plan never states what sell-side/consensus already assumes about Kalshi cannibalizing DraftKings spend, so it cannot show the finding is incremental rather than a confirmation of a widely discussed bear thesis.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Prediction-market cannibalization of sportsbooks has been an active bear narrative on DKNG since Kalshi's sports-adjacent contracts launched, discussed on calls and in sell-side notes; a rigorous internal replication of a magnitude the market has already debated is confirmatory unless the panel reveals a magnitude, timing, or cohort concentration (e.g., the H4 high-spend-user result) outside what is already assumed.
issues.what_breaks: Even a clean, statistically significant β could support a position the market has already taken, producing no incremental return despite a methodologically correct call.
issues.fix: Before the full build, record the current sell-side range/assumption for this effect (from notes or consensus models) and check whether the design — especially the H4 tenure/spend cut — is positioned to find something outside that range.

result.overall: This is an unusually rigorous, well-specified causal design with genuine falsification logic, pre-registered kill criteria, and sensible negative controls — better disciplined than most plans of this type. Its failure mode is not weak identification but fit: the econometric machinery exceeds what the stated 3-person data team and one engineer can build, maintain, or explain to a PM who must approve sizing off it, the power check that could kill the idea cheaply is buried at the end rather than gating the build, and the plan stops at a per-user causal estimate without saying how that becomes a firm-level revenue view or how it differs from what the market already assumes about Kalshi-DK cannibalization. Trim to the fixed-effects-plus-permutation-null-plus-event-study core, run power first, and add the consensus-benchmark and firm-level aggregation steps before this is actionable.

result.plan_implied_asker: A quant/systematic panel-econometrics team building an academically rigorous cross-sectional signal for its own sake, not a concentrated fundamental long/short PM who needs a fast, name-by-name defensible story.
result.what_would_falsify: Stated null: MAU adds nothing beyond lagged ARR and company trend. Explicit falsifier: refit the same specification on the excluded consumption-priced names (Snowflake, Datadog, MongoDB, Confluent) where the seat-mechanism cannot apply — if MAU predicts their revenue equally well, the thesis is sunk. Also gated on beating a two-way-FE-without-MAU benchmark out of sample via Diebold-Mariano (p<0.05) on rolling-origin and leave-one-company-out splits.

issues.summary: The full panel-econometrics stack (CIPS, Westerlund cointegration, ECM, Driscoll-Kraay, wild-cluster bootstrap, Pesaran CD, Bai-Perron) is more machinery than a ~40-cluster panel needs and more than this audience can interrogate.
issues.why_it_applies_here: With only ~40 independent company clusters (acknowledged in the plan itself), several of these tests are being pushed near or past the edge of their asymptotic justification, and no PM at a 30-person fundamental shop can push back on a Rademacher wild-cluster bootstrap or a Pesaran CD statistic — the model's credibility ends up resting entirely on the naive benchmarks bolted on for validation, making the econometric layer cost without buying defensibility.
issues.what_breaks: When a PM asks 'why do you believe this,' the analyst's honest answer collapses to the three simple benchmarks (A/B/C) and the MAPE bar — the sophisticated middle layer adds fragility (more places to have made a coding error) without adding anything the PM can independently check.
issues.fix: Keep one robust inference method (within estimator + either Driscoll-Kraay or wild-cluster bootstrap, not both) and drop the unit-root/cointegration/ECM branch unless the level-form result actually fails; let the naive-benchmark beat-test carry the argument, as designed.

issues.summary: The plan commits to full multi-vendor data licensing, two-source reconciliation, break-detection and event-logging across 35–60 names before any cheap check of whether the correlation exists at all.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Several names in the universe (Atlassian, Salesforce, HubSpot, Workday) have years of disclosed ARR and long-available web-traffic panels; a same-week scatter of published MAU growth against disclosed ARR growth for 8-10 of these would tell you the sign and rough magnitude of β before any spend on the second MAU vendor, the Wayback pricing scrape, or the break-detection pipeline.
issues.what_breaks: All of the licensing and reconciliation cost is sunk before the first falsification checkpoint (the consumption-priced-names test) is reached, so a null result arrives only after the expensive part is already built.
issues.fix: Run a 5-10 name pilot on one MAU source and disclosed ARR only; confirm sign, rough magnitude, and that it beats the naive carry-forward benchmark before scaling to the full 35-60 name, two-vendor build.

issues.summary: The price/mix-drift control (Wayback pricing-page snapshots) captures list price, which is not the realized price actually paid by the largest, most heavily-covered names in the sample.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Salesforce, Workday, ServiceNow, and Adobe negotiate custom, heavily discounted enterprise pricing that never appears on a public pricing page, while the SMB self-serve names (Zoom, RingCentral, HubSpot) do have list prices that approximate what's paid — so the exact control meant to separate 'logins changed' from 'price changed' is blind precisely for the enterprise-heavy tail of the sample, which is also where position sizes are largest.
issues.what_breaks: For enterprise names, ARR growth driven by negotiated discount or mix changes will be silently misattributed to MAU (or a real null will be masked by uncontrolled price movement), corrupting β exactly where the trading decision has the most capital behind it.
issues.fix: Split the sample by GTM motion (self-serve/list-priced vs. enterprise-negotiated) and report β and validation metrics separately, or substitute a realized-ASP proxy (RPO-per-customer, disclosed average deal size) for the enterprise subset instead of list price.

issues.summary: The plan never addresses whether MAU/app-usage panels are already inside sell-side consensus for these names, so beating a naive random-walk or FE-without-MAU benchmark does not establish the signal is unpriced.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Web-traffic-based SaaS revenue prediction using Similarweb/Sensor Tower-style panels is one of the most widely distributed alt-data theses in the industry, and Visible Alpha contributors covering these exact heavily-followed names plausibly already reference similar usage trackers when setting their ARR numbers — the plan's primary pass/fail gate (beats two-way FE without MAU, via Diebold-Mariano) is a much lower bar than beating what's already in the price, and only the secondary growth-terms check (below cross-analyst dispersion in ≥60% of quarters) actually engages consensus.
issues.what_breaks: A pass on the primary DM-test criterion could still mean the information is already fully reflected in consensus and price, so sizing a position off it risks trading an already-priced view even though the statistical test 'succeeds.'
issues.fix: Promote the consensus-beating check to the primary success criterion (not a secondary growth-terms gate), and add a short diagnostic characterizing whether the sell-side's own estimate revisions already correlate with the public MAU series before claiming the finding is actionable.

result.overall: The design is unusually careful about confounds — price/mix drift, shelfware asymmetry, tracker rebasing, panel composition, and a genuine negative control on consumption-priced names — and states a real falsifier and null. But it is built at a sophistication and scope that exceeds what a concentrated fundamental long/short shop needs or can independently evaluate, it spends most of its cost before a cheap pilot could have confirmed or killed the premise, its price-drift control silently fails exactly where enterprise pricing dominates the sample, and it never checks whether the alt-data signal is already inside sell-side consensus for these heavily-covered names. None of this is fatal — a pilot-first, price-motion-split, consensus-anchored version of the same plan would answer the question faster and more defensibly.

result.plan_implied_asker: a systematic/quant alt-data signals desk with ML engineering capacity and a diversified multi-name book, not a concentrated fundamental shop
result.what_would_falsify: Gate fails (and the plan stops, no fallback) if beta-hat is not positive and significant under the company-block bootstrap, falls outside [0.5,1.5], within-company partial correlation is below 0.45 or negative for a third of firms, or leave-one-out moves beta-hat >30% / flips significance. Conditional on a gate pass, the nowcast is 'not demonstrated' unless it beats damped persistence by >=15% RMSE, Clark-West p<0.05, and >60% directional accuracy on growth-rate change.

issues.summary: The nowcast stage (pooled fixed-effects ridge tuned by nested CV, empirical-Bayes shrinkage weighted by variance ratios) is production ML infrastructure, which the firm explicitly will not build, and it cannot be defended point-by-point to a PM the way the gate regression can.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The brief states this firm has a 3-person data team and one engineer, buys panel data, and 'will not build production ML.' A ridge model with a nested cross-validation loop and hyperparameter selection is exactly that category, distinct from the panel/cohort work the firm is described as routinely capable of.
issues.what_breaks: After the gate passes, the deliverable that actually drives position sizing (the nowcast) is a model this team cannot maintain or re-estimate reliably each quarter, and a PM cannot interrogate the ridge penalty or shrinkage weights the way they can interrogate a fixed-effects beta.
issues.fix: Use the gate-stage fixed-effects coefficient itself as the nowcast (a simple pooled-with-FE point estimate, or basic partial pooling toward the pooled mean weighted by inverse variance computed by hand), and drop ridge/nested CV unless the simple version is shown to fail on the walk-forward test.

issues.summary: The plan escalates to ridge plus empirical-Bayes shrinkage without first showing that the simpler company-FE regression already estimated in the gate stage is inadequate as a forecast.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The gate regression already produces a per-company beta and pooled beta; the walk-forward validation section could be run on that estimate directly before adding a second, more opaque model layer, but the plan moves straight to the ridge/shrinkage version.
issues.what_breaks: Extra researcher degrees of freedom (ridge penalty choice, shrinkage weighting) are introduced before the plan has shown they are needed, making the eventual RMSE improvement harder to attribute and harder to defend as not being tuned to the test set despite the embargo.
issues.fix: Run the walk-forward validation on the plain FE estimate first; only add ridge/shrinkage if that baseline demonstrably underperforms damped persistence by a margin the simple version cannot close.

issues.summary: Multiple commercial panel vendors (Similarweb, Comscore, M Science, Yipit-style, Sensor Tower, data.ai) appear to be licensed as part of the standard data build rather than added only after the gate on a primary vendor and a small seed sample (ADP, Paycom, Paylocity, Dayforce) has passed.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The gate is explicitly the kill point ('gate failure yields a negative result... not a fallback'), and the seed sample of clean seat-disclosers is small enough to test cheaply with one panel vendor; committing to a multi-vendor replication panel before that gate is decided spends licensing budget the kill criterion is designed to make unnecessary if it fails.
issues.what_breaks: If the gate fails on the cheap subsample, the replication and mobile panel licenses are sunk cost with no further use, which is exactly the spend-before-cheap-test pattern the review is meant to catch.
issues.fix: Run the gate on the primary vendor against the 4-6 cleanest seat-disclosers first; only license replication and mobile panels once that gate passes.

issues.summary: Web-traffic and app-usage panels on public SaaS names are widely subscribed commercial products, and the plan never addresses why a MAU-to-ARR nowcast built on the same vendors other funds already buy would still be mispriced.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Similarweb and Sensor Tower data on names like Dropbox, Atlassian, Asana and monday.com is standard alt-data fare in long/short SaaS coverage; the plan's consensus-surprise regression is a good empirical check but the write-up never states what current consensus assumes about this MAU-ARR link or why it would be wrong, leaving the edge case implicit rather than argued.
issues.what_breaks: If the relationship is already reflected in sell-side estimates via the same data, the surprise-regression test will correctly show no edge, but the plan will have spent the full data and modeling budget before learning that, since crowding was never assessed up front.
issues.fix: Before building the nowcast, check how many of the target companies already have sell-side or buy-side notes referencing app/web traffic data, and treat that as a cheap prior on how much of the surprise regression's power is already used up.

result.overall: The gate-and-nowcast structure is well-designed for its stated goal: it front-loads a real kill test, decomposes ARR growth into seat and price components before modeling, states explicit falsification thresholds, and works through the mechanism's failure modes (contracted vs. active seats, free tiers, enterprise blindness, disclosure endogeneity) rather than just listing generic pitfalls. The core defect is a mismatch between the sophistication of the nowcast stage and what this firm can build, maintain, and defend to a PM oss-validated ridge with empirical-Bayes shrinkage is production ML the firm explicitly rejected, and it sits on top of a fixed-effects regression that may already be a sufficient, far more explainable forecast. Trim the nowcast to the simple estimate, defer multi-vendor spend until the gate passes, and this becomes a plan the stated firm can actually run and stand behind.

result.plan_implied_asker: A systematic research/data-science team building a reusable ID-to-institution matching capability, optimizing for statistical robustness of the clustering rather than for the downstream sizing decision.
result.what_would_falsify: If the 100-permutation null (customers reshuffled at fixed institution size) is not beaten at the 99th percentile of silhouette, or cluster-wise bootstrap Jaccard falls below 0.60, or cross-window ARI falls below 0.40, the plan requires reporting the negative: only country and rough business-model separation are supportable, not named-institution identification.

issues.summary: The Hungarian-algorithm identity match — the single step where a wrong call directly causes a mis-sized position — ranks institutions by raw panel customer count against real market share, without applying the panel-composition correction the plan itself prescribes elsewhere.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan explicitly acknowledges the panel skews young/urban/digital/multi-banked and prescribes panel-reweighted shares for the feature aggregates, but the naming step ('rank IDs by panel customers, institutions by market share; Hungarian on rank distance') uses raw customer counts. A fast-growing neobank could easily out-rank a larger incumbent in raw panel presence while remaining smaller by true deposit share — exactly the kind of confidently wrong, high-conviction match the desk is most exposed to, since the margin/rank-agreement gates would pass on a systematically biased input rather than catch it.
issues.what_breaks: Tier B/C naming: a bank could clear the ≤3-candidate, rank-agreement, and margin thresholds while being matched to the wrong ticker, because the underlying panel-share ranking is biased in a known, correctable direction.
issues.fix: Apply the same panel-reweighting used for feature aggregates to the customer-count ranking that feeds the Hungarian assignment (e.g., reweight by known population/segment shares before ranking), and run the naming step both raw and reweighted — flag any institution whose tier or candidate ranking changes between the two as unresolved rather than accepted.

issues.summary: The full feature build (60-80 features, external ECB/EBA/national central bank/SPACE data) and the triple-algorithm clustering ensemble are constructed in full before the cheapest viability check (whether IDs separate at all) is run.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The silhouette/Calinski-Harabasz gate that can kill the whole approach ('<0.25 = no') only fires after the entire feature engineering and multi-source external data ingestion is complete and after Ward/GMM/HDBSCAN have all been run and reconciled — for a 1-engineer team this is substantial sunk setup before the first real signal on whether the premise holds at all.
issues.what_breaks: If IDs turn out not to separate meaningfully, the team has already built the full external-data pipeline and feature set before learning this, rather than after a cheap pilot.
issues.fix: Run a fast first pass on a reduced feature set (e.g., salary detection, balance, ATM intensity — 10-15 features) with a single clustering algorithm on a subsample of institutions to check gross separability before committing to full feature engineering and external data licensing/collection.

issues.summary: The validation stack as specified (three clustering algorithms reconciled via co-association, 500-iteration bootstrap, run independently across four six-month windows, plus a 100-permutation null) is a large compute and engineering commitment for a team of one engineer and three data staff.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The team composition given is a three-person data-cleaning group plus a single engineer; re-featuring and re-clustering 500 times per window, times four windows, times three base algorithms, is a meaningful build-and-runtime burden that isn't scoped against the team's actual bandwidth or the six-to-eighteen-month decision horizon.
issues.what_breaks: Either the full validation matrix slips the timeline past the point where the identification is useful for the horizon in question, or corners get cut on the bootstrap/window replication under time pressure, quietly weakening exactly the stability checks that are supposed to prevent false-positive naming.
issues.fix: Phase the validation: run the full stack on one window first to get a directional read, and only extend to all four windows and the full 500-iteration bootstrap for institutions that clear the first-pass gates and are actually candidates the desk wants to trade.

result.overall: This is an unusually disciplined plan for the stated purpose: it states its null explicitly, pre-commits a permutation test and stability thresholds, tiers its confidence in identity claims to match the concentrated, Type-I-dominated payoff, and pairs sophisticated clustering machinery with checks a PM can actually inspect (hand-read narratives, pre-committed rubric thresholds, explicit negative-result reporting). The one issue serious enough to block sign-off is that the final identity-matching step — the exact place where a confident wrong match does the damage the PM is worried about — ranks institutions by raw panel customer count without applying the panel-bias correction the plan uses everywhere else, which could produce a plausible-looking but systematically wrong match. Fix that, and consider a cheaper first-pass pilot before the full feature/external-data build, and this plan is fit for purpose.

result.plan_implied_asker: A fund with real (if lean) data infrastructure that can license and clean alt-data panels and is willing to spend months proving a matching pipeline is trustworthy before trading on it, treating a confidently wrong ID-to-ticker match as the catastrophic risk rather than latency, breadth, or backtested Sharpe.
result.what_would_falsify: Share of panel deposit volume assigned at ≥95% precision on held-out institutions falls below 40% for a country (declared not identifiable); permuted fingerprints failing to score at chance or phantom IDs failing to abstain (indicating the scoring is fitting noise/leakage rather than real structure); leave-one-institution-out and leave-one-country-out precision gaps that don't hold at the pre-set 0.80/0.25 margin thresholds.

issues.summary: The anchor-data build (national registries, OSM scraping, tariff PDFs, country-specific benefit-calendar joins, 500-respondent surveys) is specified as one undifferentiated requirement across five countries rather than explicitly gated to the stated pilot order (NL first, stop if it fails).
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan itself sets NL as the cheap kill test, but a 3-person data team plus one engineer will burn most of its capacity standing up DE/ES/FR/PL-specific anchors (Kindergeldnummer digits, AOW/toeslagen, CAF, INPS, tariff scraping) if that work isn't explicitly deferred until NL clears the 40% bar — undermining the very front-loaded-kill structure the pilots are meant to provide.
issues.what_breaks: Effort and calibration time gets sunk into countries whose identifiability hasn't been established yet, defeating the purpose of running NL first.
issues.fix: State explicitly that non-NL anchor acquisition and register-building only begins after the NL pilot clears its threshold, so the team's fixed capacity is spent sequentially rather than in parallel.

issues.summary: Validation is cross-sectional (leave-one-institution-out, leave-one-country-out) but there is no leave-future-quarter-out test, even though the crosswalk will be applied prospectively while positions are held for 6-18 months.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Fingerprints here are built from features like growth correlation and fee signature that are explicitly tied to a fast-moving competitive landscape (N26/Revolut/bunq growth, tariff changes) — the exact kind of thing that can drift within a single holding period, and merger/consolidation handling is addressed for the anchor side but not tested for whether the panel-side match itself degrades as a position ages.
issues.what_breaks: A match validated at time of entry could silently decay in confidence over the following two quarters without the pipeline having any test designed to catch that, and the desk would keep sizing on a mapping that's no longer as reliable as its initial acceptance criteria suggested.
issues.fix: Add a rolling/prospective check: for institutions accepted in an early quarter, re-score using only later-quarter data and report whether acceptance (p≥0.80, margin≥0.25) is stable, not just whether the initial cross-sectional holdout passed.

result.overall: This is an unusually disciplined plan for the stated problem: it fixes a falsifiable threshold up front, treats Type I error as the dominant cost via an abstain sink and high-precision gating rather than forcing assignments, keeps anchors out of the feature-building path via registers.yaml, and backs a genuinely necessary sophisticated method (optimal-transport/min-cost-flow assignment) with simple, PM-legible checks (permutation-at-chance, phantom-ID abstention, confusion matrices, risk-coverage curves). The two gaps worth closing are practical rather than conceptual: sequence the country-specific data engineering so it doesn't outrun the NL kill gate, and add a prospective/out-of-time check so a match's reliability is monitored across the holding period, not just validated at the moment of assignment.

result.plan_implied_asker: A systematic credit/quant research team building a generalizable base-rate model of guarantor-release events, with dataset infrastructure and a multi-quarter-to-year evaluation horizon.
result.what_would_falsify: Release condition matches a milestone set in the original credit/sponsor-support agreement (scheduled, not negotiated); a deconsolidation entry or VIE footnote change coincides with the release; guarantees are being withdrawn across unrelated SPVs in the same window (treasury policy, not strategy); incumbent committed spend or prepayment/reservation lines rise within two quarters either way; no independent second-source qualification and no available advanced-packaging capacity appear within twelve months; or a take-or-pay/volume-minimum/residual-value guarantee is found to have replaced the parent guarantee. The plan states the first three of these as sufficient for a confident 'no.'

issues.summary: The plan answers 'does this pattern generally indicate second-sourcing' via a 40-60 case cross-sectional base-rate study, when the actual mandate is whether this one SPV release is mispriced right now.
issues.why_it_applies_here: This desk trades one situation on a weeks-to-months catalyst; the deliverable it needs is a confident read on this hyperscaler and this chip maker, not an industry-wide likelihood ratio for guarantor-release causes. Building a stratified comparables set (fab SPVs, digital-infra SPVs, project finance) with coded triggers and a 20:1-30:1 prior is the design of a study meant to generalize, and generalizing was never the ask.
issues.what_breaks: The 'Methodology' step absorbs most of the plan's effort computing a base rate that, even if correct, only tells you what typically happens across unrelated capital structures - it does not by itself tell you whether this hyperscaler's specific action is priced.
issues.fix: Reframe the base rate as a light, secondary sanity check (a handful of truly comparable semiconductor fab-SPV releases, not three pooled asset classes) and make the primary deliverable the situation-specific chronology and falsifier read.

issues.summary: The infrastructure required - DealScan, Infralogic/IJGlobal, Bloomberg CACS/DDIS, plus registry pulls across TWSE MOPS, DART, EDINET, UCC-1/UCC-3, Companies House, Irish CRO, Luxembourg RCS, Dutch KvK and Cayman - is not something a 3-person desk with no quant staff and no dataset-building capacity can execute or maintain.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The stated context is explicit: no quantitative research staff, no capacity to build datasets, consumes sell-side/filings/expert calls. This plan requires standing up several paid specialty databases and running structured cross-jurisdictional legal searches at a scale closer to a project-finance research shop than an event-driven single-name desk.
issues.what_breaks: Analysts either cannot obtain the data (no terminal access, no registry-search workflow) or spend weeks on infrastructure instead of the primary-document read the desk is actually built to do, delaying the call past the catalyst window.
issues.fix: Cut the comparables build to what two analysts can hand-collect from public filings and EDGAR full-text search alone; drop the paid infra databases and foreign company-registry sweep unless the primary-document read leaves genuine ambiguity.

issues.summary: Computing a single Bayesian likelihood ratio (20:1-30:1, ~25x threshold) by pooling semiconductor fab JVs, data-center JVs/ABS, and classic project finance (power, LNG, toll) manufactures false precision from structurally different financing contexts.
issues.why_it_applies_here: These three strata have different guarantee mechanics, different typical triggers, and different capital structures by construction - a toll-road completion guarantee release and a fab SPV guarantee release are not draws from the same underlying process. Averaging cause-frequencies across them to get one prior is exactly the 'pooling units that should not be pooled to manufacture N' failure mode.
issues.what_breaks: The LR feeding the H1 threshold is not a real base rate for this situation; a confident 'H1 supported' or 'H1 rejected' conclusion inherits spurious precision from an invalid pooled statistic.
issues.fix: Report separate, smaller base rates by stratum (semiconductor fab SPVs only is the relevant reference class) without forcing a single blended LR, and be explicit that the semiconductor-only N will be small and judged qualitatively, not by a numeric threshold.

issues.summary: One falsifier requires waiting up to twelve months for independent second-source qualification evidence, which exceeds the desk's weeks-to-months trading horizon for this catalyst.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The firm's mandate is explicitly weeks-to-months around a catalyst with a risk manager who cuts fast; a falsifier that only resolves at 9-18 months (first silicon-proven IP, OSAT qualification) cannot inform a live position sizing decision on this timeline, even though it may be the correct falsifier in principle.
issues.what_breaks: If the desk waits for this evidence before acting, the tradeable window around the original 8-K/amendment catalyst has already closed; if it acts before the evidence arrives, the plan's own stated falsifier was never actually applied.
issues.fix: Separate the falsifiers into a near-term set usable within the trading window (documents, deconsolidation entries, portfolio sweep, spread moves) and a long-horizon confirmatory set used only to mark the thesis for later review, not to gate the initial trade.

issues.summary: The cheapest, most decisive test - checking whether the release matches a pre-specified milestone in the original credit/sponsor-support agreement (H0-a) - is written up after the expensive 40-60 case comparables build rather than gating it.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan's own 'Data' section already pulls the exact documents (Guarantee Release Date, Completion, Sponsor Support Termination definitions) needed to run this check immediately; if the release date lines up with tool move-in or first wafer-out on schedule, H0-a explains the whole event in days, making the comparables build, foreign registry sweep, and hiring-req tracking unnecessary.
issues.what_breaks: Analyst time and any paid data access get committed to the expensive base-rate and monitoring work before the cheap check that could kill the hypothesis outright has been run and confirmed inconclusive.
issues.fix: State explicitly: run the pre-commitment/schedule check first; only proceed to comparables, portfolio sweep, and independent qualification evidence if that check is inconclusive or negative for H0-a.

issues.summary: The plan never addresses what the market currently believes about this guarantor release or whether the interpretation it is testing is already reflected in price or sell-side commentary.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The desk's own framing is that the question is always whether the situation is mispriced right now, not whether the mechanism is true in some abstract sense. Nothing in the plan checks sell-side notes, prior analyst commentary on the 8-K/amendment, or current spread/equity reaction to establish that the market has not already reached the same conclusion from the same public filing.
issues.what_breaks: Even a fully confirmed H1 (independent qualification proven, spread and reservation evidence aligned) produces no trade if the market already priced the second-sourcing read off the original 8-K - the plan would confirm a correct but stale thesis.
issues.fix: Add an early, cheap step: pull sell-side notes and price/spread action around the original 8-K and the amendment date to establish whether this interpretation is already consensus before committing to the deeper primary-source program.

result.overall: The primary-source instincts here are genuine and well-suited to the desk - reading the actual guarantee, sponsor-support and credit-agreement definitions, running a portfolio sweep of the company's own guarantee footnotes, and pre-registering falsifiers that separate H1 from H2/H3 are exactly the right kind of work for a single-name event desk. But the plan escalates into a systematic, cross-sectional base-rate study (40-60 pooled comparables across three unrelated financing contexts, multiple paid specialty databases, five-plus foreign company registries, a formal Bayesian LR threshold) that neither the firm can build nor the trading horizon can wait for, and it never once asks whether the market has already reached the same read off the same 8-K. The fix is to keep the document-level chronology and falsifier logic, shrink the comparables set to a small hand-picked semiconductor-only reference class, run the cheap schedule/pre-commitment check first, and add a pricing/consensus check before spending on anything else.

result.plan_implied_asker: A single-name credit/equity special-situations desk with deep legal-document and expert-network capability, no quant infrastructure, sizing a concentrated position around a specific disclosed catalyst
result.what_would_falsify: Any two of: release language verbatim as-signed with the pre-agreed test actually met; no consent solicitation or fee found; VIE maximum-exposure-to-loss drop below the released notional; take-or-pay/reservation volumes flat or rising; no second-source qualification evidence predating the guarantor change — the plan states 'any two, no.'

issues.summary: The expensive workstreams (second-source channel corroboration across ~6 contact types, and the EL/PD-LGD sizing bridge) are not explicitly gated behind the outcome of the cheap document checks (release language, consent solicitation) that the plan itself calls 'near-dispositive.'
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan states 'cheapest disconfirmation first' as a principle but the write-up lists Documents, then Sizing, then Second-source corroboration, then Validation/killers as if all are to be executed, without a stated stop rule between them; for a two-analyst team on a weeks-to-months catalyst window, running channel calls and credit modeling in parallel with document review defeats the purpose of having a cheap kill test at all.
issues.what_breaks: If the desk commits analyst time to arranging expert calls and building the EL bridge before the consent-solicitation and release-language check has already resolved H2 vs H1/H3, the position misses its tradeable window even when the answer was available on day one from public documents.
issues.fix: Add an explicit gate: read release/completion-test language and consent-solicitation filings first; only proceed to channel corroboration and EL modeling if these do not already trigger two killers.

issues.summary: The EL bridge invokes through-cycle PD, LGD for narrow-use tooling, and rating-agency shadow methodology — a quant-credit modeling exercise heavier than what a document-and-expert-network desk without quantitative staff typically builds or defends internally.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The firm 'consumes sell-side, filings, and expert calls' and has 'no quantitative research staff' per the brief, yet this step asks the team to assign through-cycle PDs and LGDs for purpose-built shells and advanced-node tooling from scratch rather than simply comparing pre/post notional, reserve funding, and spread moves, which would likely discriminate H1/H3 from H2 just as well.
issues.what_breaks: If challenged by the PM or risk manager on where the PD/LGD numbers came from, the analysts may not be able to defend the assumptions, undermining conviction in the sizing exactly when the risk manager needs a fast, defensible answer.
issues.fix: Keep the notional/reserve/cap comparison and the SPV-spread-vs-hyperscaler-curve/CDS cross-check as the primary evidence; use the presale/shadow rating only as an input taken as given from the agency, not as a base for an internally-derived PD/LGD model.

issues.summary: The base-rate check pulls from a generic sample of 5-10 unrelated same-vintage sponsor-supported SPVs rather than first checking whether this specific hyperscaler-manufacturer pair has its own prior comparable SPV or guarantee-structure history.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The relationship is described as 'longstanding,' which makes it plausible this pair has prior capacity agreements or SPVs whose guarantee/release patterns would be far more probative of this counterparty's typical behavior than an industry sample sharing only arrangers and counsel.
issues.what_breaks: Using the generic sample as the calibration anchor when a company-specific precedent exists risks washing out exactly the idiosyncratic behavior (e.g., this hyperscaler's known aggressiveness in past negotiations) that would make the current situation atypical and tradeable.
issues.fix: Check company/manufacturer transaction history first for any prior SPV or guarantee events between the same two counterparties; fall back to the generic sponsor-SPV sample only if none exists.

result.overall: This plan is well-matched to the desk's actual toolkit and to the concentrated, Type-I-dominant nature of a single-name platform bet: it treats H2 as the modal base case to disconfirm cheaply first, states genuine falsifiers with an explicit 'any two, no' rule, and calibrates evidence to corroboration and precedent rather than demanding statistics the situation can't produce. The residual work is tightening sequencing so expensive channel and modeling work is contingent on the cheap document checks failing to resolve the question, trimming the credit-model machinery in the EL bridge to something two document-driven analysts can defend unaided, and checking this counterparty pair's own SPV history before reaching for an unrelated industry sample.

result.plan_implied_asker: a systematic multi-strategy quant fund with production NLP/ML infrastructure, judged on net-of-cost alpha, capacity and crowding, with a committee that independently re-runs results
result.what_would_falsify: Residual peer-relative tone (after orthogonalizing against SUE, 3-day announcement return, momentum, and style factors) fails to predict forward risk-adjusted returns in the pre-registered, single-touch 2023-2024 holdout; or net-of-cost/capacity-adjusted alpha falls below the stated 30bp breakeven; or the 2023-2024 vs 2015-2018 alpha comparison shows the effect has decayed to zero. The plan explicitly states a clean null is an acceptable, real output rather than something to be explained away.

issues.summary: The expensive infrastructure build (domain-adaptive MLM over 1.5-2B tokens, 6,000 hand-annotated sentences, 150k LLM silver labels) is committed before the near-free version of the same test — LM dictionary tone or off-the-shelf FinBERT regressed on peer-relative forward returns — is run as a gate.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan itself designates LM/FinBERT as the 'baseline to beat' and includes them in the final ablation table, which proves they are cheap to compute from the same parsed transcripts already required for the pipeline — so the capability to run the cheap check first already exists, it's simply scheduled at the end instead of the front.
issues.what_breaks: If the simple dictionary/off-the-shelf tone signal shows no relationship to peer-relative returns after orthogonalization, the weeks of domain-adaptive training and the annotation project were sunk before that information was available.
issues.fix: Run LM tone and vanilla FinBERT through the full peer-relativization, orthogonalization, and portfolio-construction pipeline first, as a one-week pilot. Only commit to domain-adaptive MLM training and the annotation project if that pilot shows a signal worth refining.

result.overall: This plan is well-matched to the firm and the question: it is a genuine cross-sectional signal test with point-in-time data discipline, an explicit null and falsifier, honest multiple-testing correction (HLZ threshold, deflated Sharpe, specification counting) sized to the actual number of cuts it runs, and cost/capacity/crowding treated as primary outputs rather than afterthoughts — exactly what a systematic committee needs to re-run and trust. The one real defect is sequencing: the cheap version of this test (dictionary or off-the-shelf sentiment against peer-relative returns) is available immediately from the same data and is used only as a late-stage baseline instead of a first-week gate before the domain-adaptation and annotation spend is committed.

result.plan_implied_asker: a systematic factor-research team pre-registering a single candidate signal with hard statistical gates before committing production infrastructure spend
result.what_would_falsify: Any one of: tone t<2.5 two-way-clustered (rising to 2.9 Bonferroni if three tone variants reported); net-of-cost annualized spread <3% or IR<0.4; correct sign in fewer than 7 of 10 years (excluding Mar-Dec 2020) or t<2.0 on that count; or the effect concentrated in the bottom size quintile (>=40% of spread) / absent in >=2 of 4 size quartiles. Any single failure triggers the two-page kill memo rather than the infra build.

issues.summary: The primary test window ([+2,+63] trading days, 60-day holds, monthly rebalance) runs to roughly a quarter, well past the firm's stated days-to-weeks trading horizon, and the plan never reconciles this before scoping a production build on pass.
issues.why_it_applies_here: This firm is explicitly described as trading days to weeks with in-house execution tuned for that cadence; a signal that only shows incremental t beyond the immediate reaction window and needs a ~quarter hold to realize the spread is a genuinely different book (turnover, capacity, execution cost profile) than what the stated infrastructure and mandate imply, and the days 11-14 'build scope' step does not ask whether a slower-turnover sleeve is even wanted or how it nets against the firm's existing capacity allocation.
issues.what_breaks: If the signal passes the gate, days 11-14 default straight into infrastructure/latency/capacity build without first checking whether a 60-day-hold factor fits the execution and capital-allocation framework this firm actually runs, risking build effort on a signal that doesn't fit the book it would need to live in.
issues.fix: Add one explicit branch condition at the gate: before day 11, confirm with the desk that a quarterly-turnover signal is wanted, or re-test the decay curve at higher frequency (does information content survive a shorter 20-30 day hold, which would fit the mandate better) before committing build resources.

result.overall: This is a well-built plan: it matches the goal (establishing a broad cross-sectional effect), fits the firm's infrastructure and review process, treats crowding and decay as the central risk rather than an afterthought (vendor client-count calls, McLean-Pontiff-calibrated prior, 2004-2010 replication requiring a much higher t), and pairs sophisticated panel econometrics with simple checks a research committee can verify itself (sign-count over years, vendor rank-correlation, placebo and shuffled-label tests). Sequencing is entropy-reducing - cheap crowding checks and pre-registration before any data touch, early-period replication before the full cost-loaded backtest - and the kill criteria are specific, quantified, and stated before the data is examined. The only real gap is that the tested holding period runs to roughly a quarter while the firm's stated horizon is days to weeks, and the plan does not check that mismatch before scoping an infrastructure build on a pass; everything else here should be approved close to as written.

result.plan_implied_asker: A quantitative empirical-asset-pricing research group with event-study and intraday-data infrastructure, closer to a systematic factor-research desk than a fundamental PM shop.
result.what_would_falsify: Pooled announcement-window β below 20bp peer-relative abnormal return per 100bp revision with t≤5 (first-stage gate) kills the project outright; separately, a placebo (30-day-shifted) coefficient that does not vanish, or failure of sign/magnitude to replicate in the pre-committed 2015-2025 holdout, is stated as grounds to reject H1/H2.

issues.summary: The reverse-causality check requires TAQ intraday tick data and the infrastructure to build 2-hour signed-return windows, which this firm explicitly does not have.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The brief states the firm has no tick data or execution infrastructure and will not build production ML; the plan's Identification section nonetheless calls for TAQ-based pre/post-activation signed-return comparisons from 2010 onward, which a three-person data team and one engineer cannot build or maintain.
issues.what_breaks: The reverse-causality/leakage check in Identification cannot be executed as specified, leaving the causal-timing claim (revision precedes price action, not the reverse) unverified for the entire post-2010 sample.
issues.fix: Drop the TAQ component and rely on the daily-data reverse-window CAR(-5,-2) leakage test already in the Validation section, which uses data the firm already licenses.

issues.summary: Three redundant structural-instability estimators (Wald/bootstrap across regime buckets, Bai-Perron sup-F, Kalman-filtered beta path) plus a full Fama-MacBeth/2SLS/BH-correction stack are layered onto a single stability question no PM can independently adjudicate.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The desk explicitly requires output defensible to a PM asking 'what would have to be true for this to be wrong' — a question answerable from one pre-registered regime-interaction test, not from reconciling three different, routinely-disagreeing instability estimators and a DCF-fed 2SLS specification; a three-person data team plus one engineer is also not equipped to build and maintain this stack indefinitely.
issues.what_breaks: If Bai-Perron, the variance-ratio test, and the bootstrap disagree — common with these three on the same series — there is no stated rule for which governs, so the PM cannot resolve a disagreement the plan itself will produce.
issues.fix: Keep the single pre-registered Wald/bootstrap test on the four named regime buckets as primary evidence; demote Bai-Perron and the Kalman path to an unreported robustness appendix.

issues.summary: The plan never engages with the fact that analyst-revision-driven re-rating and revision drift are among the most heavily mined regularities in equity research, so it never establishes what would be incremental if H1/H2 come back significant.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The DV/IV pairing here (peer-relative EV/EBITDA re-rating on FY1/FY2 consensus revisions) is a close cousin of decades-old estimate-revision and post-revision-drift factors already embedded in many systematic books and sell-side revision screens; a clean significant result here could simply be recovering that well-known, already-priced pattern in a new wrapper, and no step in the plan checks this.
issues.what_breaks: Even a statistically pristine H1/H2 result gives the desk no basis to know whether it is proprietary or already reflected in how peers price revisions, so position sizing built on it risks sizing into a crowded pattern.
issues.fix: Add a step comparing the magnitude/persistence found here to published performance of generic revision/drift factors (or to the fund's own past experience trading around revisions on held names), and state explicitly what about this construction — peer-relative, EV/EBITDA-specific, 24-month constant-horizon — would survive where the generic factor has decayed.

issues.summary: The plan stops at panel-level coefficients (β, β*, regime interactions) and never specifies how a finding from this panel becomes an actual sizing adjustment on a specific held position.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The desk context is explicit that output should change position sizing on named companies, yet every deliverable in the Estimation and Validation sections is an industry/panel-level statistic (Fama-MacBeth coefficients, Kalman beta paths, calendar-time drift portfolios) with no stated step mapping 'stock X just had a same-analyst FY2 EBITDA revision of Ybp in regime Z' into a sizing decision for stock X.
issues.what_breaks: The study can conclude the mechanism exists and describe its properties but leaves no operational bridge to what a PM changes about a given position tomorrow, so the work risks being informative without being directly actionable in the stated use case.
issues.fix: Add a final translation step: given estimated regime-conditional β and β*, define a simple per-name overlay and demonstrate it on a handful of current book names as a worked example.

result.overall: The plan does real, careful work fixing the circularity in the question as posed and builds in genuine pre-committed kill criteria (feasibility gate, first-stage β threshold, placebo, split-sample), which is exactly the right instinct for a concentrated fundamental book where false positives are costly. But as written it is scoped and instrumented for a systematic research desk with tick-data infrastructure and a bench of econometricians, not for a 30-person fundamental shop with one engineer and three data staff, and it never confronts whether a revision-driven re-rating finding would be anything other than a well-known, already-priced pattern, nor how the panel-level result becomes a sizing decision on a specific name. Strip the TAQ dependency, collapse the three redundant instability tests to one, add a crowding/incremental-edge check, and add a worked per-name translation step, and this becomes a plan the firm can actually run and a PM can actually use.

result.plan_implied_asker: a systematic quant-research team with dedicated econometrics infrastructure and long build timelines
result.what_would_falsify: β1 statistically indistinguishable from zero or wrong-signed across the FE/clustering specs; the 500-draw placebo peer-reassignment fails to collapse β1; ΔCAGR(t+1) pre-trend is significant (implies confound, not response); or the out-of-sample (2012+) quintile-sort spread is insignificant/decaying — any of these would abandon or substantially qualify H1.

issues.summary: The tests most likely to kill the whole approach (mechanical EV/EBITDA identity decomposition, placebo peer reassignment) are embedded mid- and late-plan rather than run first as a cheap gate before the full multi-region, multi-vendor, 20-year panel is built.
issues.why_it_applies_here: DV (Δlog EV/EBITDA_NTM) and the EBITDA-CAGR regressor share the same EBITDA tape by construction; if the identity check shows the relation is mostly mechanical (β_multiple negligible relative to β_EV), all downstream FE/clustering/shrinkage/robustness work is moot, but this is only discovered after the full data build and estimator are running.
issues.what_breaks: Resources are sunk into constructing point-in-time snapshots across Russell 3000 + MSCI World ex-US back to 2005 before the cheapest, most diagnostic check has been run on a small sample.
issues.fix: Run the identity decomposition and a single-region, single-quarter pilot regression first as a go/no-go gate before commissioning the full global point-in-time build.

issues.summary: The full data build (four-plus vendors, two regions, ~20 years, point-in-time constituency including dead/acquired names, IFRS16 adjustment) is a large sustained engineering project for a three-person data team plus one engineer.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The firm's stated capability is licensing and cleaning alt-data panels and running panel/cohort studies, not maintaining a multi-vendor, multi-region, two-decade point-in-time consensus and fundamentals infrastructure with definitional harmonization (adjusted vs reported EBITDA, IFRS16 breaks) — that is closer to what a systematic multi-factor shop staffs for.
issues.what_breaks: The data build itself could consume the team's bandwidth for a quarter or more before any regression output exists, pushing the usable answer well past what a PM sizing positions over a 6-18 month horizon can wait for.
issues.fix: Pilot on a single region (US) and single primary consensus vendor across a handful of the highest-conviction industries first; extend to ex-US and additional vendors only after the core β1 is confirmed material.

issues.summary: The plan never checks whether the historical growth-revision-to-rerating relationship is still exploitable now, versus being a well-known, already-crowded pattern that has decayed.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Growth/EBITDA-revision-driven multiple re-rating closely overlaps the long-standing 'estimate revision' factor already used across systematic and increasingly fundamental strategies; a pooled 2012-present OOS statistic can be significant purely because the effect worked a decade ago and says nothing about whether it is still tradable today.
issues.what_breaks: The practical validation step reports one pooled spread/t-stat from 2012; if the spread is concentrated in the earlier years and has been shrinking, the PM will size positions off a stale edge presented as current.
issues.fix: Split the OOS quintile-sort validation into rolling 3-5 year sub-windows and require the most recent window to still show a material, significant spread before it is used to size positions.

issues.summary: H1's core claim — that measured elasticity is below the DCF-theoretical elasticity because the market treats revisions as partly transitory — is asserted as market underreaction without testing whether that skepticism is actually correct.
issues.why_it_applies_here: If large ΔCAGR revisions in fact reverse at a high rate in subsequent quarters, the market's muted reaction is rational pricing of noisy signals, not underreaction, and trading against it would be adverse selection rather than edge — the plan never distinguishes these two stories even though the data needed (does N2Y CAGR actually materialize k quarters later) is already in the panel.
issues.what_breaks: The economic-validation step compares measured β1 to theoretical elasticity and calls a lower ratio 'coherent,' but a lower ratio is equally consistent with correct market discounting of unreliable revisions, which would invalidate the trade thesis even though the regression passes every stated diagnostic.
issues.fix: Add a persistence check — track whether large ΔCAGR revisions are confirmed or reversed k quarters later — to separate genuine underreaction to durable growth from correct discounting of noisy forecasts.

result.overall: This is a well-constructed mechanism test — it anchors magnitude against a DCF benchmark, builds in a mechanical-identity check, a placebo, negative-control industries, and a simple quintile-sort validation the PM can actually read, which resolves the sophistication-versus-audience tension reasonably well. The two real gaps are proportionality and edge durability: the full multi-vendor, two-region, twenty-year infrastructure is sized for a systematic research desk rather than a three-person data team, and it is built before the cheap circularity/placebo gate is run, and the plan never checks whether this revision-driven re-rating pattern is still exploitable now rather than a known, decaying effect. Neither is fatal, but both should be resolved with a cheap single-region pilot and a recency/decay cut before the full build is committed.

result.plan_implied_asker: A systematic/quant research team with dataset infrastructure, event-study modeling capability, and time to build and validate statistical pipelines — not a lean discretionary catalyst desk.
result.what_would_falsify: If stage-one shows the check-driven optimism is already reflected (two of three: full-year consensus revision >~0.5%, (0,today) CAR at/above the estimation-window SD and arithmetic-implied CAR, straddle-implied move already >1.2x trailing 8-quarter realized median), the pricing leg fails and the long is rejected. Separately, if stage-two's guidance-policy history shows management does not raise the full year at this point in the calendar (base rate and pass-through too low relative to the straddle), the conversion leg fails and the long is rejected. Both must be wrong (checks unpriced AND guidance likely to move) for the long case to survive.

issues.summary: Stage one requires building a multi-vendor dated event log and running a two-factor CAR event study with standard errors, dispersion metrics, and a regression of historical CAR on guidance-revision size — infrastructure this desk has explicitly said it cannot build or staff.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The brief states no quantitative research staff and no capacity to build datasets, yet the plan's own stage one is a dataset-construction and statistical-modeling exercise (Bloomberg/Refinitiv pulls, two-factor model, SE-based thresholds), and stage two adds a CAR-on-guidance-revision regression on top — none of which the PM, two analysts, or the fast-acting risk manager can independently build, audit, or defend under time pressure.
issues.what_breaks: The pricing-gap conclusion in stage one and the expected-value sizing in stage two rest on machinery nobody on the desk can sanity-check; if a coefficient, window choice, or comp basket is mis-specified, the error propagates into a position size with no internal check capable of catching it before the risk manager has to act.
issues.fix: Substitute a version native to the team's actual toolkit: raw relative price performance vs. 2-3 direct comps since the information date, plus the headline consensus revision from an off-the-shelf Visible Alpha/Bloomberg snapshot. Reserve the full two-factor/SE event study only as an escalation if that simple read is genuinely ambiguous, and only if someone on the desk can actually own and defend the build.

issues.summary: The formal two-factor CAR event study is specified as the default first move in stage one rather than as a fallback after a simple price-vs-comps and consensus-revision check.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan's own pitfalls section admits the underlying check data is a non-random, undersized, denominator-less sample — directional only — so a formal econometric event study is unlikely to sharpen the conclusion much beyond what an eyeballed relative-price move and headline consensus revision would already show, yet it is written as the primary test rather than something reached for only if the cheap version is inconclusive.
issues.what_breaks: Analyst time and calendar days go into building the dated event log and dual-specification event study before knowing whether the question was ever close enough to need that precision, eating into the runway before the print.
issues.fix: Run the simple check first as an explicit go/no-go gate (rough comp-relative move, headline consensus revision magnitude); escalate to the full two-factor/SE build only if that result lands in a genuine grey zone.

issues.summary: Stage-one gate thresholds (>0.5%, <0.2%, 1.2x trailing 8-quarter median) are stated as decision-grade cutoffs without being derived from this stock's own volatility or revision history.
issues.why_it_applies_here: This is a single-name, single-event call with no cross-sectional sample to calibrate a threshold against; asserting a precise breakpoint like 0.5% vs 0.2% manufactures false statistical precision that a thin, non-random check-based dataset cannot actually support, and a print landing near the line gets adjudicated by an arbitrary number rather than judgment.
issues.what_breaks: A situation sitting at, say, 0.4% consensus revision gets mechanically routed to 'priced' or 'not priced' by an uncalibrated cutoff, potentially killing or advancing the trade on a coin-flip line rather than a considered read.
issues.fix: Treat the numbers as heuristics, not hard gates — require explicit PM sign-off on borderline cases, and calibrate thresholds against this stock's own historical revision-to-price relationship from its prior beat/raise episodes rather than a generic percentage.

result.overall: The framing is right for this desk — decompose the long case into 'is it priced' and 'will guidance move,' use the company's own guidance history rather than a cross-sectional base rate, and default to no unless both legs fail — and the plan states a real, falsifiable gate with genuine engagement with the disconfirming case. But the execution imports a systematic-research toolkit (multi-vendor event logs, two-factor CAR studies with standard errors, CAR-on-guidance regressions) that a three-person discretionary desk with no quant staff and no dataset capacity cannot build, audit, or defend fast enough for a risk manager who cuts positions quickly. Strip stage one down to a simple, inspectable price-versus-comps and consensus-revision check, reserve the econometrics only if that is ambiguous, and treat the numeric gates as judgment aids rather than precise cutoffs.

result.plan_implied_asker: A quant-equipped shop with data-engineering capacity and modeling staff, treating point-estimate precision as the main risk — not a lean two-analyst catalyst desk.
result.what_would_falsify: Three explicit falsifiers are named: (1) the 8-quarter backtest showing channel commentary is positive 6/8 times but raises guidance only 3/8 times — 'signal is uninformative — stop'; (2) at the print, if FY revenue impact is <75bps vs midpoint, <50bps vs consensus, the raise is ≤1.5x the median prior Q2 raise, or capacity/cRPO checks fail, skip the print entirely; (3) post-entry, cRPO deceleration, weak customer adds, a raise at/below flow-through, falling land value, an 8% price stop, or failure to move within two sessions post-print all trigger an exit.

issues.summary: Alt-data sourcing (LinkedIn/job postings, cloud-marketplace listings, G2 velocity, HG Insights/Enlyft) and the quant build (12Q bottom-up reconciliation to 1%, least-squares ramp-curve fit, 4-parameter Monte Carlo) require dataset engineering and modeling skill this desk explicitly does not have.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The context states this desk has 'no quantitative research staff and no capacity to build datasets' and 'consumes sell-side, filings, and expert calls' — the alt-data workstream and the fitted-curve/Monte-Carlo machinery are exactly the dataset-building and quant-modeling work that was ruled out, not a generic objection about complexity in the abstract.
issues.what_breaks: Either the alt-data/Monte-Carlo steps don't get built in time for the 'upcoming print,' leaving the thesis untested at the catalyst, or building them consumes the two analysts' entire window and crowds out the primary-source/expert-call work this desk is actually equipped to do well.
issues.fix: Drop the LinkedIn/G2/HG Insights/Enlyft build and lean on the sell-side and expert-call reads already planned; replace the least-squares-fitted ramp curve and Monte Carlo with a hand-built bull/base/bear scenario table (logo delta x land value x lag) that two analysts can construct and a non-quant PM can check line by line.

issues.summary: The cheapest test capable of killing the whole thesis — the 8-quarter backtest of channel commentary against actual guidance outcomes — is sequenced after the expensive bottom-up model and data build rather than before it.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The backtest only needs the '3 years of transcripts tagged for guidance language' and prior guidance history already on the data list; the plan's own stated result ('positive checks 6/8 times but raises only 3/8: the signal is uninformative — stop') is exactly the entropy-reducing test that should gate whether the rest of the work is worth doing, yet it is written up in the validation stage after the reconstruction/ramp-curve/Monte-Carlo methodology has already been laid out.
issues.what_breaks: Analyst time gets spent reconciling 12 quarters of revenue to 1% and fitting a ramp curve before learning the channel-check signal may carry no incremental information for guidance at all — the one finding that would make the rest of the build moot.
issues.fix: Run the transcript-vs-guidance backtest first, using only data already in hand, before committing to the bottom-up reconstruction, alt-data purchases, or Monte Carlo; only proceed to the heavier model if the backtest clears the bar.

issues.summary: The initial ramp-curve seed R(0)≈max(0,(45−L)/90) is an unexplained linear parametrization that anchors the headline '<75bps' conclusion before any fitting occurs.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The entire in-year-vs-not-catalyst call rests on how fast a new logo ramps into revenue; a specific linear form with unexplained 45-day and 90-day constants can shape what the least-squares fit converges to given only 8-12 quarters of data, so the '<75bps, inside noise' conclusion may reflect the seed's shape as much as the company's actual ramp behavior.
issues.what_breaks: The reported p10/50/90 for FY revenue bps will look precise while partly reflecting the parametrization choice, and the ≥75bps go/no-go gate could trigger or miss on that artifact rather than on real ramp economics.
issues.fix: Show the FY-bps conclusion is robust to at least one alternative functional form (e.g., a step function seeded directly from the cohort-chart bins) before relying on the point estimate to gate the trade.

result.overall: The core design is well matched to this desk's mandate — it separates the print catalyst from the twelve-month ARR thesis, states a real variant view against sell-side channel-check extrapolation, uses the company's own eight-quarter record rather than a cross-sectional base rate, and gates entry and exit on explicit, checkable thresholds. The defect is that this good design is wrapped in a quant build (dataset scraping, least-squares curve fitting, Monte Carlo) that a two-analyst, no-quant-staff desk was told it cannot support, and the one cheap test that could kill the idea outright — the historical backtest of channel commentary against actual guidance — is buried behind that build instead of run first. Strip the alt-data and simulation layers, run the backtest before anything else, and the plan delivers what this firm actually needs on the timeline it has.

result.plan_implied_asker: a systematic multi-strategy quant desk building a cross-sectional signal meant to survive cost, capacity and crowding scrutiny before sizing
result.what_would_falsify: Two explicit gates: (1) if RLOIB's Fama-MacBeth coefficient, controlling for ALLOIB and RETOIB, has |t|<2.0 at every horizon (1,5,20 days), the round-lot filter adds no information beyond known retail proxies and the idea dies; (2) if it survives that but the net-of-cost long-short alpha has t<2.0 under base cost assumptions, the effect is real but unharvestable and the tradeable version is abandoned.

issues.summary: No direct test of whether the effect is already crowded, despite the firm explicitly judging signals on crowding.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Retail order-imbalance-predicts-reversal is a well-published effect (subpenny/odd-lot retail proxies have circulated in academic and practitioner literature for years); the plan tests RLOIB's incrementality over RETOIB/ALLOIB and checks cost/capacity, but never asks whether the incremental round-lot signal itself has been decaying or is already being harvested by other desks, which is one of the three things this firm explicitly evaluates on.
issues.what_breaks: A signal could clear the incremental-information gate and the net-alpha gate yet still be a decaying, already-arbitraged effect that will not survive live because everyone with TAQ access can build the same lot classifier.
issues.fix: Add an explicit within-sample decay/trend test on the incremental coefficient and net alpha (e.g., rolling-window coefficient plot, alpha by year), and treat a monotonic decline as evidence of crowding rather than only using the 2019/2021 splits as structural-break checks.

issues.summary: The 100-share round-lot threshold is held fixed through the present even though the SEC's later tiered round-lot redefinition changes what "round lot" means for a subset of securities.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan's own pitfalls section admits the threshold is stale for part of the sample, and this bites hardest in exactly the low-price, less-liquid names where round lots are meant to proxy retail activity most cleanly \u2014 the tiering change alters lot-size meaning precisely in the subsample the signal depends on.
issues.what_breaks: RLOIB's classification of "round" versus "odd" flips meaning for tiered securities post-change, contaminating the most recent data with a measurement discontinuity that a single fixed-threshold z-scored panel will not separate from genuine signal decay.
issues.fix: Recompute RLOIB using the security-specific tiered definition for the post-change period and run it as a distinct robustness bucket rather than folding it silently into the main fixed-100 panel.

result.overall: This is a well-built plan for the stated audience: it tests the retail-proxy assumption rather than asserting it, sequences a cheap incremental-information gate before the costly portfolio and capacity work, states two real falsification thresholds, and matches the firm's cost/capacity-centric evaluation standard with a full spread-plus-impact model and breakeven output. The two gaps worth fixing are secondary rather than blocking: no explicit test for whether the incremental effect is decaying/crowded (one of the firm's three stated criteria), and the round-lot threshold's known staleness under SEC tiering is flagged but not resolved for the recent sample. Neither undermines the core design; both are addressable without re-architecting the plan.
