result.plan_implied_asker: a large systematic multi-strategy firm with deep tick-level infrastructure and a research committee that reruns everything, for whom the main risk is a mined or crowded signal rather than a wrong single-name call
result.what_would_falsify: Failure of any single gate across every tested partition kills the identification claim: G1 lift <2.0x or bootstrap lower bound <1.5x; G2 recall <35%; G3 signing accuracy <70% (hard stop <60%); G4 mean stock-day correlation vs Benchmark A <0.40 or vs Benchmark D <0.25; G5 panel |t| <3 on forward-return regression. Even if all pass, Phase 2 (the profitability claim) is separately falsified by after-cost Sharpe <1.0, any negative year, or net/gross <0.40.

issues.summary: Universe filters (price $3-$600, ≥250k median daily volume) are not specified as point-in-time or trailing, risking a full-sample look-ahead selection into which names qualify for the round-lot/retail identification test.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The study spans 36 months and uses volume/price screens to fix a static 2,000-2,500 name universe; if these are computed over the whole window rather than rolling, the sample over-represents names that were reliably liquid throughout, which is exactly the population where institutional VWAP/TWAP slicing into round lots (the H0 mechanism) is most active, biasing the lift/recall estimates in the direction of the null.
issues.what_breaks: The universe construction step biases G1/G2 gate estimates toward whichever regime (institutional-slicing-heavy large caps) dominates a full-period-computed liquidity screen.
issues.fix: Reconstruct the universe on a rolling (e.g., quarterly) basis using only trailing volume/price data, or report the gate results separately for a fixed-at-start-date universe vs an ex-post one to bound the bias.

issues.summary: Phase 2's forward-return continuation test does not specify the horizon over which returns are measured, leaving the plan unable to confirm it targets the firm's stated days-to-weeks mandate rather than an intraday/seconds-scale effect that would require different infrastructure to monetize.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Retail-order-imbalance continuation effects in the literature range from minutes (liquidity provision) to weeks (return drift); this plan's mechanism (round lots, sub-penny TRF prints) sits naturally at the very short end, while the firm trades days-to-weeks, so the horizon at which Phase 2 will test continuation determines whether a pass is even actionable for this firm.
issues.what_breaks: If Phase 2 is greenlit and the continuation signal turns out to live at seconds-to-minutes horizons, the firm's days-to-weeks execution and portfolio construction cannot capture it despite a technically passing gate.
issues.fix: Pre-specify the forward-return horizon(s) for the Phase 2 decile sorts and Fama-MacBeth regressions before Phase 2 begins, and tie the choice explicitly to the mechanism tests (price elasticity, notional clustering) already planned in Phase 1.

issues.summary: The Hui-Walter latent-class estimate used in G1 assumes conditional independence between the imperfect labels (sub-penny TRF pricing, RLP flags, Rule 605 buckets), which is questionable since several of these labels share a common cause (wholesaler PFOF routing practices) rather than being independent measurements of the same latent retail state.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Benchmarks A and B/C are not independent instruments here — sub-penny price improvement and RLP certification both arise from the same wholesaler internalization mechanism, so treating them as conditionally independent inputs to a latent-class model will overstate the precision of the combined estimate rather than genuinely triangulating it.
issues.what_breaks: G1's lift/precision figure, and by extension the pass/fail decision to proceed to Phase 2, could be inflated by correlated-error mislabeling rather than reflecting true identification accuracy.
issues.fix: Report the pairwise correlation of disagreement between benchmarks A, B, and C before running Hui-Walter, and if conditional independence is violated, either drop the latent-class step in favor of the direct Rule 605 accounting figure alone or use a dependent-label extension of the model.

result.overall: This is a well-built plan for the stated audience: it correctly separates the identification claim from the profitability claim, front-loads the cheapest possible kill test (Rule 605 accounting) before committing to tick-level data engineering, states a genuine falsifiable H0 with a mechanistic rationale for why round lots might now signal institutions rather than retail, and matches the committee's sophistication with methods it can rerun and corroborate. The remaining gaps — unclear point-in-time universe construction, an unspecified horizon for the eventual continuation test, and an unexamined independence assumption in the latent-class benchmark combination — are real but secondary; none of them would change the decision to run Phase 1 as designed.

result.plan_implied_asker: A well-staffed fundamental research team with bandwidth for multi-decade, cross-industry historical data collection and detailed accounting-forensics modeling — not a 2-analyst desk with no database support.
result.what_would_falsify: Negative on any of: negative implied gross bookings two straight quarters; channel inventory >1.5x normal; a backlog/LTA definition change in a quarter that would otherwise have declined; supplier finished-goods inventory rising two quarters while backlog is called record.

issues.summary: The validation plan calls for a full backtest across four unrelated historical shortage episodes (memory/passives 2017-18, semis 2021-22, AI-cycle components, telecom 2000), which duplicates and contradicts the plan's own stated calibration source.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan already says haircuts are 'calibrated from the prior episode's (2021-23 semiconductors) realized backlog conversion, using worse company history where it exists' — a single, well-chosen analog. Requiring a separate ground-up backtest across telecom (2000), memory/passives (2017-18) and an undefined 'AI-cycle' basket on top of that imports breadth-study logic into what is explicitly single-name research, and demands data collection (peer backlog/LTA/realized-revenue history across four industries and two decades) that a two-analyst shop with no database cannot assemble without months of effort.
issues.what_breaks: The 'Validation' step balloons into a multi-industry historical study before the single-name question is answered, consuming analyst time that the firm does not have relative to its 25-30 position, buy-and-hold model.
issues.fix: Use the already-named semiconductor 2021-23 episode as the primary calibration set, treat the other three as optional, lower-effort sanity checks (a handful of hand-picked comparables, not a full reconstruction), and only build them out if the semis analog produces an ambiguous or contested tier calibration.

issues.summary: The plan lists cheap disqualifying checks (RPO sign/plug diagnostics, mirror-disclosure reconciliation, cross-supplier double-ordering) alongside the full buildout rather than sequencing them first.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Several of the stated negative criteria (negative implied gross bookings, backlog/LTA definition changes, mirror recon <50%) can be checked directly from a handful of filings before the agreement register, six-attribute scoring, segment-level coverage math, and 10-15 year capex depreciation schedule are built — yet the plan presents 'data required' and 'methodology' as one undifferentiated block with no stated order, meaning the expensive machinery gets built regardless of what the cheap checks would have shown.
issues.what_breaks: A single analyst could spend the bulk of the available time building the agreement register and capex schedule before discovering, from a cheap RPO/mirror check, that the thesis is already dead — sunk cost that a five-person shop cannot easily absorb.
issues.fix: State explicitly: run the RPO-plug sign check, the double-ordering cross-check, and the mirror-disclosure reconciliation first; only proceed to the full agreement register, tiering, and capex schedule if none of those trip the stated negative criteria.

issues.summary: The coverage ratio's denominator ('modeled revenue per quarter') is never defined or sourced, leaving open whether it is independent of the backlog/RPO inputs used in the numerator.
issues.why_it_applies_here: If 'modeled revenue' is itself derived from company guidance or extrapolated off the same backlog/RPO trend being measured, coverage = haircut-adjusted committed revenue ÷ modeled revenue becomes partly circular — a denominator that moves with the regressor — which the plan's own stringent thresholds (60% NTM Tier 1/2 coverage, 40% year-two coverage) would then be gating on an inflated or self-confirming ratio.
issues.what_breaks: The coverage thresholds that decide constructive vs. negative could be met or missed for a mechanical reason rather than a genuine change in commitment strength.
issues.fix: Specify that modeled revenue comes from an independent bottom-up or consensus estimate built without reference to the RPO/backlog series, and show the two are constructed from non-overlapping inputs before applying the coverage thresholds.

result.overall: This is a well-built single-name plan: it matches the concentrated long-only firm's real risk (being wrong about the business, not costs), stays in public-filing/Bloomberg territory the firm can actually execute, produces an IC-inspectable bridge rather than a black box, states genuine falsifiers, and engages seriously with the bear case (reflexivity, enforcement weakness, duration-vs-growth confusion). The defects are calibration, not conception: the validation section over-reaches into a multi-industry historical study that contradicts the plan's own stated calibration source and exceeds what two analysts can realistically build, and the cheap kill checks (RPO sign, mirror recon, double-ordering) are not sequenced ahead of the expensive buildout they could render moot. Trim the historical backtest to the named semis analog, front-load the cheap negative-criteria checks, and clarify the coverage-ratio denominator, and this becomes a genuinely lean, defensible piece of work for this desk.

result.plan_implied_asker: A multi-strategy or systematic research desk with dedicated data-science and legal-research staff building a reusable cross-cycle diagnostic framework, not a concentrated fundamental shop needing one call on one holding
result.what_would_falsify: Episodes where contracted price stayed materially above spot for 8+ quarters post-normalization, absent a hard qualification moat, would falsify the 'bimodal, switching-cost-driven' hypothesis.

issues.summary: The plan builds a general cross-industry mechanism test but never specifies the step that classifies the actual subject company's own switching-cost/qualification-lag regime, so the finished framework has nowhere to attach to the single-name call the firm actually needs.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The firm holds 25-30 concentrated names and needs a durability verdict on one guidance event; the plan's hypothesis explicitly says outcome is 'split by switching cost, not contract language,' yet no step gathers the subject company's own contract terms, customer concentration, or requalification process to place it in a bucket alongside the 20-30 reference episodes.
issues.what_breaks: The final 'probability-weighted haircut' output has no defined mapping back to the company being evaluated, so the IC receives a general framework instead of a position-specific answer.
issues.fix: Add an explicit first sub-step: classify the subject company's product against the switching-cost axis using its own 10-K/Exhibit-10 disclosures and industry structure, and name the 3-5 closest analogs before deciding how much of the broader episode set is needed.

issues.summary: The data and legal infrastructure the plan requires (TrendForce, Fastmarkets, UxC, Argus/ICIS, Drewry/Xeneta, Panjiva/ImportGenius, PACER, Delaware Chancery, ICC/SIAC filings) is well beyond what a five-person shop with no data scientists, no database maintenance, and only occasional data purchases can acquire, reconcile, or maintain for one position.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The firm profile states it has two analysts, one operations person, no engineers, and buys research 'occasionally' — this plan calls for standing up roughly eight paid specialized data feeds plus multi-jurisdiction litigation research, which is a due-diligence unit's workload, not a single analyst's project on a single holding.
issues.what_breaks: The plan as scoped cannot actually be executed by 'one analyst' as required; it either stalls mid-build, requires unbudgeted outside spend, or gets partially executed and delivered as an incomplete, unverifiable dataset to the IC.
issues.fix: Restrict the data diet to free/already-owned sources (EDGAR filings, press, Bloomberg pricing, published litigation summaries) for a shortlist of 3-5 closest analogs; only license a paid feed if that shortlist leaves the direction genuinely ambiguous.

issues.summary: The cheapest, most decisive step — determining which switching-cost regime the subject company's product falls into — is scheduled after building the full 20-30 episode database, contract coding, and per-market capacity ledgers, rather than first.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan's own causal claim is that qualification lag, not industry label, determines the outcome (aerospace forgings and LNG hold, polysilicon and containers reprice) — that classification is answerable from the company's business description in days, independent of the other 29 episodes, yet the plan puts months of database-building ahead of it.
issues.what_breaks: Expensive data licensing and cross-jurisdiction legal research proceeds before confirming whether the answer is already obvious from the company's own switching-cost profile, risking sunk effort on work the classification step would have made unnecessary.
issues.fix: Do the company-specific classification first as a standalone one-week exercise; only proceed to full episode-matching, capacity ledgers, and holdout validation if that classification is contested or ambiguous.

issues.summary: Building a full capacity ledger (fab additions, ramp curves, hidden capacity) and customer breach-arithmetic model for every reference market is more machinery than a directional durability call for one holding requires.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Capacity-ledger construction demands SEMI fab-database tracking and capex-guidance monitoring across eight-plus unrelated end markets in parallel, which a single analyst cannot sustain alongside normal coverage duties, and the plan never shows that a simpler check (current spot-vs-contract spread on the subject company's own disclosed peers) fails first.
issues.what_breaks: Analyst time gets consumed maintaining ledgers for markets that have no bearing on the one position being evaluated, delaying the answer the IC actually needs.
issues.fix: Limit capacity-ledger work to the subject company's own end market; use the other episodes only for qualitative pattern-matching on switching cost, not full ledger replication.

result.overall: The hypothesis is sharp, the falsifier is real, and the plan engages the disconfirming case seriously — but it is built at the scale and with the infrastructure of a systematic research team's cross-cycle study, not a one-analyst answer to a single guidance event at a 25-30 name concentrated book. The core diagnostic (does this company's product sit in a hard- or easy-requalification regime) is knowable cheaply and should come first; instead it is buried behind a 20-30 episode, multi-jurisdiction, multi-vendor-data build the firm cannot staff or maintain. Scale the framework down to the 3-5 closest analogs and the subject company's own filings before any data licensing or legal research is committed.

result.plan_implied_asker: A concentrated fundamental long-only analyst with a multi-quarter to multi-year holding horizon, working from public filings and price lists, who needs every number traceable by hand and defensible to an IC that cannot inspect a model — not a shop worried about latency, crowding, or transaction costs.
result.what_would_falsify: If the bottom-up model, run retroactively on the last known renewal, fails to predict the realized margin move within stated error bars, or if the central-case estimate lands under ~25bps even on the adversarial (half-size) reading, the 'stronger risk than communicated' thesis is rejected and the defensive tone is treated as noise.

issues.summary: Step 3's comparable-customer uplift distribution assumes access to other customers' confidential renewal terms without specifying how a two-analyst shop actually obtains it.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Every other input in the plan is named and public (10-K tables, GSA/Crown Commercial schedules, vendor price lists, RFP postings, LinkedIn headcount), but the '5-10 similar customers renewed in 24 months' distribution is the single number the Step 5 inversion is compared against, and actual per-customer negotiated uplifts are rarely disclosed anywhere public — this firm has no data function and only buys research occasionally, so the sourcing method for exactly this input needs to be stated, not assumed.
issues.what_breaks: If the Step 3 distribution is thinly sourced or guessed, the Step 5 inversion ('compare required uplift to Step 3's distribution') inherits false precision and the central-case call rests on a number the IC cannot check.
issues.fix: Name the sourcing method explicitly (e.g., a small number of expert-network channel checks with IT procurement contacts at comparable customers, or reseller channel checks) and cost it as a discrete step; if it can't be sourced, collapse Step 3 to the price-list/RPO-growth proxy alone and say so rather than presenting a distribution built on unstated inputs.

issues.summary: The prior-renewal backtest and the Step 4 history reconstruction likely draw on the same one or two known data points, so the 'validation' risks being partly in-sample rather than an independent check.
issues.why_it_applies_here: With only 2-3 prior renewals for this specific vendor-customer pair, using 'the prior renewal' both to calibrate expectations (Step 4, reconstructing what management said versus what happened) and then to validate that the framework 'predicts the realized move within error bars' risks testing the model against the same episode it was informed by, particularly if Step 4's observed inflection pattern quietly shapes the phasing and uplift ranges fed into Step 5.
issues.what_breaks: A backtest that passes because it was fit to the same episode gives false confidence in the framework heading into the live renegotiation, when the real test is whether it predicts an episode it never saw.
issues.fix: If more than one prior renewal exists, hold at least one out entirely from calibration and backtest only against that one; if only a single prior renewal exists, state plainly that the check is a consistency check rather than independent validation and weight it accordingly in the final call.

result.overall: This plan is well-matched to the firm and the question: it discards the confounded signal (tone), substitutes a directly measurable target (margin bps and EPS impact), sequences cheap size-it-first work ahead of granular contract analysis, stays entirely within Bloomberg/filings/Excel-level technique an IC can inspect, and commits to real falsification thresholds plus an adversarial review and survivorship-bias correction. The two gaps worth fixing — unspecified sourcing for the comparable-customer uplift distribution, and a backtest that may partly reuse its own calibration data — are fixable without redesigning anything and neither is blocking.

result.plan_implied_asker: A well-resourced systematic/quant research group with data engineering staff, multi-vendor data licensing budgets, and ML infrastructure, building a durable cross-sectional NLP signal for a broad book — not a five-person concentrated fundamental shop asking about one company's one earnings call.
result.what_would_falsify: For the general mechanism: H2 false — the elevated evasiveness score shows no out-of-sample predictive power for GM surprises (|t|<2.5, no sign lift over base rate), consistent with the stated modal outcome that caginess reflects NDA/legal constraints with no informational content. No separate falsifier is stated for the actual decision the IC needs — what specific case-specific finding (e.g., flat purchase obligations, stable vendor pricing, no supplier-language redlines) would clear this company of the risk regardless of the transcript score.

issues.summary: The question is about one company's one event; the plan answers it by building a generalizable cross-sectional signal across a ~40,000 firm-quarter panel.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The IC asked whether THIS company's margin risk is understated, not whether executive evasiveness predicts margin surprises on average across the market. Even a validated H2 only tells you the average lift across thousands of firms; it does not by itself answer the specific question, and the plan never closes that gap with a company-specific inference step.
issues.what_breaks: The historical-test and validation stages produce a market-wide statistic; the step that would actually answer the IC's question (how to read this company's score given the population result) is never specified.
issues.fix: Reframe as a single-name study: use the company's own trailing-call baseline and its own purchase-obligation/supplier disclosures as primary evidence, and treat any cross-sectional panel work as optional corroboration, not the deliverable.

issues.summary: The infrastructure required (pinned LLM classifiers, embeddings, elastic-net logistic models, Driscoll-Kraay SEs, Romano-Wolf correction, five outcome/data vendors, 1,500 hand-labels) cannot be built, staffed, or maintained by a five-person shop with no engineers or data scientists.
issues.why_it_applies_here: This firm buys research and datasets occasionally but explicitly cannot operate infrastructure or maintain a database. The plan requires standing up an NLP pipeline, licensing Visible Alpha/IBES/Compustat/CRSP/two transcript vendors, and running a pre-registered panel study — months of quant research capacity this firm does not have and one analyst cannot execute alone.
issues.what_breaks: Every stage past the transcript read requires tooling and vendor integration the firm has no path to acquire or run reliably, so the plan stalls or gets outsourced, defeating the point of an internal read on one holding.
issues.fix: Drop the panel and modeling apparatus entirely; keep only what one analyst can do in Bloomberg/Excel/filings — read the transcript, pull the purchase-obligations table and Item 1A language, check vendor/customer filings.

issues.summary: An IC that is explicitly skeptical of models it cannot inspect will not accept a decision built on elastic-net logistic regression, embedding-based classification, block-bootstrapped panel coefficients, and Romano-Wolf multiple-testing correction.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The mandate states the IC must be able to inspect and defend the method. None of the core machinery here (pinned LLM labels, elastic net, two-way clustering plus Driscoll-Kraay) can be explained or verified by a PM in a committee meeting, regardless of how well it performs statistically.
issues.what_breaks: Even a strong, correctly-validated result cannot be presented to the IC in a form it will trust enough to act on, so the entire pipeline produces an output the firm cannot use.
issues.fix: Replace with something the IC can eyeball: side-by-side transcript excerpts from this call vs. prior calls on vendor questions, the purchase-obligations trend, and a plain-English read of supplier/customer filings — a corroborating simple check, not a substitute model.

issues.summary: The cheapest, most decisive evidence — this company's own trailing eight calls, its purchase-obligation tables, Item 1A supplier language, and vendor/customer filings — is placed last, as a 'case-specific' addendum, after the entire systematic panel is built.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Per the evidence hierarchy, a company with a documented history of vendor negotiations should be judged on its own record first; that record is available today in filings and can be read in a matter of days, yet the plan schedules it behind data licensing, hand-labeling, and a 40,000-firm regression.
issues.what_breaks: Months and multiple vendor contracts are committed before the one piece of evidence most likely to answer the question — or kill the idea — is even examined.
issues.fix: Start with the company-specific read: compare this call's vendor Q&A to its own trailing baseline by hand, pull the purchase-obligations and supplier-language trend, and only escalate to broader methodology if that evidence is genuinely ambiguous.

issues.summary: A validated panel-level relationship (|t|≥2.5 across ~40,000 firm-quarters) does not tell you whether this specific company's elevated score is a true signal or one of the many false positives implied by an average effect of that size.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The panel test manufactures statistical power by pooling firms that are not the firm in question; per-company confidence given a population-level coefficient is a distinct, unaddressed inferential step, and the plan never states how a lift measured in basis points across the panel translates into a probability statement about this one holding.
issues.what_breaks: The final output the analyst hands the IC would be a market-wide regression coefficient, not a calibrated read on the company being evaluated.
issues.fix: State explicitly, before running the panel, what post-hoc mapping from population lift to single-firm probability would be used — or skip the panel and rely on within-firm consistency (does this company's own history show the same pattern preceding real deterioration) instead.

issues.summary: The plan never states what the market currently believes about this company's margin trajectory or why sell-side/buy-side positioning has it wrong.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Even if 'management is being evasive' is measured perfectly, that alone doesn't establish an edge — if the vendor renegotiation and its margin implications are already discussed in sell-side notes or reflected in consensus GM estimates, the finding is confirmatory, not actionable, however rigorously produced.
issues.what_breaks: The recommendation to the IC would rest on a measurement without ever checking whether the risk is already priced.
issues.fix: Before or alongside the transcript work, pull the last few sell-side notes and consensus GM revisions on this name to establish what's already assumed, and frame the finding as incremental to that.

result.overall: The methodological instincts (placebo topics, out-of-sample split, human-rated validation, known-outcome falsification) are sound in isolation, but the plan is built at the scale and sophistication of a systematic multi-sleeve quant study when the actual question is a single-name underwriting call for a five-person shop with no data-science capability. The cheap, decisive evidence — this company's own call history and its purchase-obligation/supplier filings — is buried behind months of infrastructure the firm cannot build, staff, or defend to its IC. Kill the panel and the classifier pipeline; the question is likely answerable in days using the case-specific materials alone, with the systematic work adding cost and opacity without adding something this firm can act on.

result.plan_implied_asker: A systematic/quant desk validating a scalable cross-sectional alt-data factor with data engineering support, not a concentrated fundamental shop.
result.what_would_falsify: Equal out-of-sample predictive accuracy on the excluded consumption-priced (negative-control) names as on the seat-based panel, or failure of the MAU model to beat the two-way fixed-effects benchmark under Diebold-Mariano (p<0.05) with the stated MAPE/median-YoY-error bars not met — the plan explicitly says this sinks the thesis.

issues.summary: The plan is architected as a systematic factor-validation study (multi-vendor panel econometrics, scaling capital, decay curves by cap size) rather than a due-diligence tool a concentrated fundamental shop can run.
issues.why_it_applies_here: This firm has no data scientists, nobody maintains a database, and infrastructure is Bloomberg+Excel+filings; the plan requires merging multiple paid alt-data panels (Similarweb, Datos, Verto, Sensor Tower/data.ai) and Visible Alpha line items into a maintained, point-in-time-stamped ~1,000-row panel with splicing and structural-break logic — exactly the standing infrastructure this five-person shop cannot operate.
issues.what_breaks: The data acquisition/merge step and its ongoing maintenance; nothing downstream can run without it, and the analyst assigned has no realistic path to build or sustain it alongside normal coverage.
issues.fix: Scope down to the 2-5 seat-based names actually in or considered for the portfolio, pulled by hand from a single vendor each quarter, and drop the cross-sectional panel-econometrics apparatus entirely.

issues.summary: The estimation and validation stack (CIPS unit-root, Westerlund cointegration, ECM, Driscoll-Kraay, wild cluster bootstrap, Pesaran CD, Bai-Perron, Diebold-Mariano) is far beyond what this IC can evaluate or challenge.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The audience is explicitly skeptical of models it cannot inspect and has no quant background; none of these tests can be explained in an IC meeting in a way that lets the committee verify the claim, so the conclusion runs on authority rather than the transparency this firm's decision culture requires.
issues.what_breaks: The validation/gating step becomes a black box the IC either rubber-stamps or rejects wholesale regardless of merit, and no one on the desk can rerun or sanity-check it next quarter.
issues.fix: Make the plan's own simple benchmarks (A/B/C carried-forward and trailing-growth comparisons) the headline test, present them as an inspectable scatter/table per name, and keep the econometric machinery as an internal footnote, not the gate.

issues.summary: Web/app usage panels predicting SaaS revenue is one of the best-known alt-data strategies of the last decade, and the plan never asks whether this is already priced or crowded among users of the same vendor data.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The deliverable is graded against beating sell-side consensus (Visible Alpha dispersion, Diebold-Mariano vs. a no-MAU benchmark) — a genuine alpha claim — using vendors that quant/alt-data desks have mined against these same tickers (Atlassian, Salesforce, Zoom, HubSpot) for years; without addressing that, a positive result could just mean the market already knows this.
issues.what_breaks: The interpretation of a passing beta/DM test; the plan would treat 'MAU forecasts ARR' as investable information when it may already be embedded in consensus via the same panel data.
issues.fix: Check whether current sell-side revisions already track MAU inflections with a lag; if so, state that the edge, if any, is in earlier/exclusive access to the panel, not in the existence of the relationship.

issues.summary: The plan commits to acquiring and merging multiple paid data panels and building a ~1,000-row point-in-time database before running any cheap sanity check of the core relationship.
issues.why_it_applies_here: This firm buys research and datasets occasionally rather than running standing multi-vendor infrastructure, so simultaneously licensing Similarweb, Datos, Verto, Sensor Tower and Visible Alpha is real, avoidable spend for a shop this size, committed before anyone has checked whether MAU and ARR even move together for a single held name.
issues.what_breaks: Budget and analyst time get sunk into infrastructure before the premise is checked; if the relationship is weak for the names that matter to this book, the spend was wasted.
issues.fix: Start with one vendor and the 2-5 relevant portfolio/watchlist names, plot log MAU against log ARR by quarter, and only expand to the full panel and additional vendors if the pattern is visibly present.

issues.summary: The design is built and gated as a quarter-ahead earnings-surprise tool rather than a check on a multi-year business thesis.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Positions are held three to five years and the desk's risk is being wrong about the business, not missing a quarterly beat; a tool tuned to out-predict sell-side estimates one quarter ahead, with language about scaling capital and decaying edge by cap size, answers a shorter and different question than whether a specific company's growth is durable.
issues.what_breaks: Success criteria (median YoY error vs. consensus dispersion each quarter) reward short-horizon forecasting accuracy that may say little about whether portal engagement confirms or undermines a multi-year thesis on a specific holding.
issues.fix: Reframe the deliverable around trend consistency over 8-12 quarters for the specific held name(s) — does MAU direction confirm or diverge from the ARR trajectory the thesis depends on — rather than single-quarter forecast-beat metrics.

issues.summary: The core mechanism assumes MAU-per-seat and price-per-seat drift slowly enough that MAU maps to seats/ARR, but this link is never directly validated against actual seat counts because none are disclosed.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Per-seat SaaS vendors frequently bundle seat packs, migrate tiers, or allow shared logins, so an MAU move can reflect utilization change with no seat or ARR implication; the plan's mitigations (Wayback price index, shelfware interaction) patch specific known failure modes but never test the primary MAU-to-seats assumption itself.
issues.what_breaks: The estimated beta could be picking up utilization-only variation rather than the seat/ARR relationship the thesis claims, and none of the stated guards are designed to catch that.
issues.fix: Where seat counts are disclosed even occasionally (investor days, S-1s, call remarks), spot-check the MAU-to-seat ratio's stability for a subset of names before trusting the panel-wide elasticity.

issues.summary: The panel pools structurally different businesses (Workday HR software, Zoom video, Adobe creative tools, Asana project management) into one elasticity via company fixed effects, which can average away exactly the differences that determine whether the mechanism holds for any one holding.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Within-company fixed effects estimate a single average beta across names whose portal usage patterns, admin-vs-end-user login mix, and seat-definition conventions differ substantially, so a pooled beta of 0.4-0.8 could reflect which names dominate the panel rather than a reliable per-name relationship — precisely the substitution a concentrated book cannot afford when the risk is being wrong about one business.
issues.what_breaks: Applying the panel-average beta to a specific holding assumes that holding behaves like the average sampled name, undermining the single-name conviction this firm actually needs.
issues.fix: Report per-company betas for each name in or near the portfolio and use the pooled result only as a prior, never as the number applied to any single holding's ARR call.

result.overall: This is a technically careful mechanism test written in the vocabulary and infrastructure of a systematic alt-data desk, not a five-person concentrated long-only shop with no data science capacity and an IC that distrusts models it cannot inspect — the panel-econometrics stack, multi-vendor data buildout, and quarter-ahead consensus-beating framing are all mismatched to how this firm actually loses money (being wrong about one business over years, not missing a quarterly print). It also never asks whether app-usage-panel-predicts-SaaS-revenue is already common knowledge among users of the same vendors, which is the question that determines whether a positive result means anything. The idea itself is worth pursuing in a far cheaper form: pull one vendor's MAU series against disclosed ARR for the 2-5 seat-based names this firm actually holds or is considering, eyeball the relationship and its exceptions, and only build further if that holds up.

result.plan_implied_asker: A systematic research team with data-engineering capacity, built to validate a nowcasting signal across a broad SaaS coverage universe and beat consensus on a quarterly cadence, where a false positive is absorbed across many small bets.
result.what_would_falsify: Gate fails if beta is not positive/significant under the block bootstrap, falls outside [0.5,1.5], within-company partial correlation is below 0.45 pooled or not positive for two-thirds of firms, or leave-one-out moves beta more than 30% / flips significance -- this yields a stated negative result plus a taxonomy of failure modes, not a fallback to naive MAU-vs-revenue. For the secondary nowcast, RMSE reduction under 15% vs damped persistence or a Clark-West p >= 0.05 is labeled 'not demonstrated.' This is a genuine, well-specified falsifier -- one of the plan's real strengths.

issues.summary: The plan requires multiple paid panel vendors, device-graph calibration, scraped pricing histories, a point-in-time vintage database, and custom econometrics code (fixed-effects panel, Driscoll-Kraay SEs, block bootstrap, ridge with nested CV) that this five-person shop has no engineers, data scientists, or database function to build or maintain.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The brief states explicitly that nobody at the firm maintains a database and there are no engineers or data scientists; this plan's very first gate step already requires standing up a multi-vendor point-in-time data pipeline and running custom statistical code, which is precisely the capability the firm lacks.
issues.what_breaks: The methodology section cannot be executed by one analyst on Bloomberg/Excel/filings as required; the project stalls at data acquisition/calibration long before the gate is ever tested.
issues.fix: Rescope to a single already-accessible data source (or none) and a within-company Excel-based comparison for the 2-3 SaaS names the firm actually owns or is diligencing, dropping the multi-vendor panel and custom econometric pipeline entirely.

issues.summary: The core inferential machinery (Driscoll-Kraay SEs, 2,000-draw block bootstrap, empirical-Bayes shrinkage ridge, Diebold-Mariano with Harvey-Leybourne-Newbold correction, Clark-West) is uninspectable by the audience, and no simple check is offered that lets the IC verify the actual conclusion themselves.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The firm is explicitly described as an IC skeptical of models it cannot inspect; the plan's only 'sanity checks' (G2/Gartner fields) validate data quality, not the inferential claim itself, so the decision-relevant result still rests entirely on machinery nobody at the firm can defend or challenge.
issues.what_breaks: Even a fully passing gate produces a number the IC must take on faith rather than verify, so it cannot actually carry a position decision -- which is the stated purpose of the work.
issues.fix: Make the primary artifact a plotted YoY MAU-growth-vs-YoY-ARR/seat-growth series per held company that an analyst can eyeball and an IC can question directly; keep the panel econometrics, if pursued at all, as an appendix-level robustness check rather than the gate itself.

issues.summary: The entire validation apparatus targets quarter-ahead nowcast accuracy and beating sell-side consensus surprise, which is a short-horizon trading signal, not evidence relevant to a business held for three to five years.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The firm holds 25-30 concentrated positions for three to five years and is told to care about being wrong on the business, not about trading around prints; the plan's success bar (RMSE reduction vs damped persistence, Clark-West significance, directional accuracy on the growth-rate change, consensus-surprise regression) is calibrated entirely to next-quarter forecasting value, which this firm has no use for.
issues.what_breaks: A signal that clears every quarterly-nowcast gate still says nothing directly about whether the multi-year seat-growth trajectory underlying the investment thesis is intact, so the validated output does not answer the question the PM actually needs answered.
issues.fix: Reframe success around whether multi-quarter MAU trend/inflection corroborates or contradicts the multi-year thesis for a held name, not quarterly RMSE or consensus-beat metrics.

issues.summary: The plan never argues why this specific approach would find something not already known: the named companies (Atlassian, Asana, monday.com, Dropbox, Smartsheet) are among the most heavily traded alt-data names precisely because web/app usage panels on them have been used by quant and event-driven funds for a decade.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Similarweb, Sensor Tower and comparable panels on exactly these tickers are a well-known, crowded alt-data trade; the plan states no variant view against consensus and no argument for why its use of the same vendors on the same names would be incremental.
issues.what_breaks: Even a statistically significant pooled result most likely confirms a relationship the market -- and specifically funds that specialize in this data -- already prices, so acting on it risks buying a crowded read rather than a genuine edge.
issues.fix: State explicitly what would be incremental here -- e.g. restrict to a name or engagement metric the sell side and other alt-data users do not track -- or reframe the exercise as a diligence corroboration tool rather than a source of edge.

issues.summary: Pooling businesses with structurally different seat dynamics (enterprise HR/payroll seats like ADP/Paycom/Dayforce versus PLG collaboration seats like Asana/monday.com/Dropbox) into one fixed-effects panel manufactures cross-sectional N and inverts the evidence hierarchy that should favor a held company's own multi-quarter record.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan's own pitfalls section admits contracted-vs-active-seat and free-tier dynamics differ by business model, yet the primary gate is a single pooled beta and a pooled partial correlation threshold rather than a per-company or per-cluster estimate, which is what actually matters for a concentrated stock-picker deciding on one name at a time.
issues.what_breaks: A pooled pass licenses trust in MAU data for a specific holding even if that name sits in the failing third of the within-company correlation distribution or belongs to a business-model cluster the pooled average does not represent.
issues.fix: Report per-company or per-business-model-cluster estimates as the primary decision input for any single position, and demote the pooled statistic to background context.

issues.summary: Substantial data-acquisition and calibration spend (multiple vendor licenses, device-graph work, scraped price histories, vintage database construction across roughly a dozen companies) is committed before the cheapest possible look at whether the relationship has legs.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Given the firm's stated inability to operate this kind of infrastructure, the cost of reaching even the first gate is already large and largely sunk before any result is seen, whereas the firm could check the core idea on the 2-3 names it actually holds with one already-accessible data source first.
issues.what_breaks: Resources are spent building a research infrastructure the firm cannot reuse or maintain, before there is any evidence the idea is worth pursuing at all.
issues.fix: Run a one-week pilot on the 2-3 owned/diligenced SaaS names with a single cheap data source, eyeball MAU growth against disclosed seat/ARR growth, and only scale to the multi-vendor panel and econometrics if that pilot looks promising.

result.overall: This is a well-constructed piece of applied econometrics with a real, pre-committed falsifier and a sensible proxy-validation gate -- but it is written for a systematic shop with data engineering and a quantitatively literate committee, not for a five-person concentrated long-only manager with no database function and an IC that must be able to inspect what it is shown. The infrastructure, statistical machinery, and quarterly-nowcast success criteria all mismatch this firm's capability, oversight needs, and multi-year holding horizon, and the pooled cross-sectional design buries the per-holding evidence that would actually matter for an underwriting decision. The question can be answered far more cheaply: pull one accessible traffic proxy for the names the firm actually owns and plot it against disclosed seats/ARR before building any of this.

result.plan_implied_asker: A systematic quant fund with engineering and data-science staff building a scalable, capacity-constrained cross-sectional factor across the full equity universe
result.what_would_falsify: Stated directly: peer-relative tone residual shows zero incremental risk-adjusted return beyond SUE, 3-day announcement return, momentum and style-factor controls in the pre-registered 2023-2024 holdout, or break-even trading cost falls below roughly 30bp — the plan explicitly treats a clean null as a real, acceptable output.

issues.summary: The entire pipeline requires infrastructure (Snowflake/Xpressfeed ingestion, GPU domain-adaptive transformer training, TAQ tick data, five-way point-in-time database merges, LLM silver-labeling, annual walk-forward retraining) that a five-person shop with no engineers, no data scientists, and no one maintaining a database cannot build, run, or maintain.
issues.why_it_applies_here: This isn't a generic 'quant is hard' objection — specific steps named in the plan (domain-adaptive MLM on 1.5-2B tokens, dual-head encoder training, Krippendorff-alpha-gated human annotation cascades, RDQ/GICS/CRSP/Compustat/I-B-E-S point-in-time merges) each individually require skills and systems this exact firm profile states it does not have.
issues.what_breaks: Every step from transcript parsing through model training through the walk-forward retraining loop; none of it is a one-analyst, Bloomberg-and-Excel task, so the plan cannot be executed as written by this firm regardless of whether the hypothesis is true.
issues.fix: Replace the custom transformer pipeline with an off-the-shelf sentiment/tone tool (or a licensed vendor score) applied to a short list of names the analysts already follow, run in Excel/Bloomberg, with no model training or database infrastructure required.

issues.summary: The deliverable is a diversified quintile long/short factor with an IR, capacity curve and crowding analysis, which is a systematic-book output with no stated translation into a buy/hold/sell call on one of the firm's 25-30 concentrated positions.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The portfolio construction step (GICS/TNIC peer quintiles, EW/VW long-short, Fama-MacBeth alpha, capacity-where-net-alpha-halves) is built for a book with breadth; this firm holds 25-30 names for 3-5 years and cannot run a rebalancing quintile long-short sleeve, so a proven residual-tone effect still leaves the IC with no answer to the only question it asks — is this specific business being misjudged.
issues.what_breaks: The Portfolio and Validation sections produce a tradable systematic signal that has no mapping back to single-name underwriting; the firm cannot act on 'this stock is in the top quintile of peer-relative tone this quarter' the way it acts on a thesis about a business.
issues.fix: Reframe the deliverable around the firm's actual unit of decision: for names held or under active review, does tone deviation on that company's own calls (versus its own history, not a cross-sectional peer quintile) coincide with subsequent fundamental deterioration the analyst can verify against filings.

issues.summary: The plan never states what is incremental about this specific construction versus the already-published, already-crowded literature on earnings-call NLP sentiment that it itself cites (Cao/Jiang/Wang/Yang, Loughran-McDonald).
issues.why_it_applies_here: The pitfalls section names 'managers writing for machines' and treats crowding/break-even cost as a result to be measured at the end rather than a prior to be argued up front; nowhere does the plan explain why peer-relative Q&A-tone-deviation would still carry information after a decade of academic and vendor factors targeting the same transcripts.
issues.what_breaks: Even a statistically clean, well-validated positive result would be indistinguishable from 'we successfully re-discovered a factor everyone already has,' since no consensus/crowding baseline is established before the test is run.
issues.fix: Before building anything, check whether existing vendor sentiment scores (already licensed by many funds) already price this; if a simple off-the-shelf score shows the same pattern, the edge is gone and the expensive custom pipeline is moot.

issues.summary: A domain-adapted transformer with silver-labeled LLM annotations, dual-head architecture, Fama-MacBeth regressions and Harvey-Liu-Zhu deflated Sharpe thresholds is not inspectable by an investment committee that is explicitly skeptical of models it cannot inspect.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The IC's stated bar is defensibility against models it can't examine; nothing in this design — not the transformer weights, not the silver-label cascade, not the multiple-testing-corrected t-stats — can be explained or defended in an IC meeting the way a fundamental thesis can, even though simpler benchmarks (LM, FinBERT) exist inside the plan and could have been the headline instead of an ablation footnote.
issues.what_breaks: At presentation, the IC either takes the black-box result on faith (which they've said they won't) or the entire multi-quarter build is unusable for its stated purpose of informing IC decisions.
issues.fix: Lead with the simplest interpretable measure (e.g., Loughran-McDonald tone deviation, which is a transparent word-count ratio) as the primary result the IC can audit by hand on a sample of calls, and treat the transformer only as an internal robustness check, not the headline.

issues.summary: The cheap, fast falsifier — whether a plain lexicon-based tone measure shows any peer-relative return relationship at all — is available almost immediately but is only run as one line in a later ablation table, after the expensive transformer pretraining and annotation pipeline is already built.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan itself lists LM/FinBERT as 'baselines to beat' in the ablation section, which is scheduled after the domain-adaptive MLM training (1.5-2B tokens, multi-epoch) and the annotation/silver-labeling cascade — meaning the step most likely to kill or validate the idea cheaply sits behind the most expensive infrastructure build rather than gating it.
issues.what_breaks: Months of model-training and labeling cost are committed before the cheapest available test of the core hypothesis (does any tone measure correlate with peer-relative returns) has been run and inspected.
issues.fix: Run the lexicon-based peer-relative tone regression first, on a manageable subsample, as a go/no-go gate; only proceed to domain-adaptive transformer training if the crude version shows a pattern worth refining.

issues.summary: The primary signal horizon (1-3 months, tested out to 12) is calibrated to a post-earnings-drift-style decay, which is structurally irrelevant to a firm holding positions 3-5 years.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Even a fully validated 1-3 month peer-relative outperformance signal answers a different question than the one this firm needs answered when underwriting a 3-5 year holding — the plan never states how a short-horizon quintile signal should inform a multi-year thesis, so the horizon chosen serves the factor-test goal, not the stated use case.
issues.what_breaks: A positive, robust result would still leave the analyst with no guidance on whether to buy for the next five years, since the tested effect is explicitly short-lived and untested at the firm's actual holding horizon.
issues.fix: If a case-level version of this is pursued, test whether tone deviations on a company's own calls predict deterioration in the specific KPIs the analyst underwrites over one to three years, not peer-relative price drift over one to three months.

result.overall: This is a well-built, technically careful design for testing a cross-sectional NLP factor — but it is the wrong plan for this firm on every axis that matters: it requires infrastructure and staff the firm does not have, produces a diversified systematic output that doesn't map onto a 25-30-name concentrated book, and never argues why this construction would find edge in an already well-mined corner of the literature. The falsification criterion and null-is-a-real-outcome framing are genuine strengths, but they validate the wrong deliverable for this audience. A one-analyst version — off-the-shelf tone scoring applied to the firm's own watchlist, checked by hand against filings — would answer the question this firm actually has in days, not quarters.

result.plan_implied_asker: a systematic multi-strategy quant team with WRDS-grade database infrastructure, evaluating whether a cross-sectional factor is worth building or licensing for systematic execution
result.what_would_falsify: Explicitly stated and layered: tone t<2.5 clustered (rising to 2.9 under Bonferroni across three tone variants); net long-short spread <3% annualised or IR<0.4; correct sign in fewer than 7 of 10 years, or 2004-2010 replication t below 2.0 ex-2020; bottom size quintile driving ≥40% of the spread or sign failing in more than one of four size quartiles; effect confined to [0,+1] fails; a t of 2.1 is named outright as a kill. This is a genuine, pre-committed falsifier, not a hedge.

issues.summary: The entire pipeline (WRDS, Capital IQ transcripts, CRSP/Compustat/I-B-E-S, point-in-time GICS, Hoberg-Phillips TNIC-3, decile-panel regressions with two-way clustering) requires database infrastructure this firm has no capacity to build or maintain.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The context states explicitly there are no engineers, no data scientists, and nobody maintains a database here; tooling is Bloomberg, Excel, and filings. This is not a generic 'quant work is hard' objection - the plan names WRDS pulls, point-in-time GICS, and TNIC-3 alternative peer construction as required inputs, none of which a Bloomberg/Excel shop can source or refresh.
issues.what_breaks: Day 4 ('Data') cannot be executed by 'one analyst' as the brief requires; the firm would need to hire a contractor or buy a finished dataset, which changes the entire cost and control structure of the exercise before day 1 is even reached.
issues.fix: Redesign the data step around what Bloomberg/FactSet/vendor exports and manual transcript pulls can actually deliver for the 25-30 names the firm holds or is evaluating, or explicitly scope this as a purchased, turnkey vendor score evaluation rather than an in-house cross-sectional build.

issues.summary: The plan validates a systematic, tradable cross-sectional factor (Russell 3000, decile sorts, monthly-rebalanced long-short, capacity/licensing branch) when the firm's actual decision unit is a single business held concentrated for three to five years.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Nothing in the 14-day plan produces an output usable by an analyst building a thesis on one of the firm's 25-30 holdings - there is no step that asks 'does this quarter's tone on Company X's call, relative to X's own history, corroborate or contradict our thesis on X.' The deliverable at pass is infrastructure/licensing scope for a decile long-short sleeve, which this firm does not and cannot run.
issues.what_breaks: Day 10 and the pass branch (days 11-14) produce a factor product or vendor-licensing decision that has no place in a 25-30 name concentrated book; the IC receives nothing it can act on even if every kill criterion is cleared.
issues.fix: Reframe the pass condition around single-name usability: e.g., a validated rule of thumb ('within-firm tone deterioration beyond X, net of guidance and surprise, has historically preceded margin/thesis breaks in Y% of comparable cases') tested first against the firm's own historical holdings, with the Russell-3000 panel used only as a secondary corroboration, not the primary deliverable.

issues.summary: The statistical machinery (Fama-MacBeth with Newey-West, two-way clustered panel regressions, industry-by-quarter fixed effects, Harvey-Liu-Zhu Bonferroni adjustment, FF5 factor decomposition) is not something this IC can inspect or defend.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The brief states the IC is 'skeptical of models it cannot inspect.' This is a materially higher bar of technique than an OLS-with-clustering check a fundamental IC could interrogate line by line; multiple-testing-adjusted t-statistics and factor-loading robustness tables are not defensible in that room regardless of whether the underlying research is sound.
issues.what_breaks: Even a clean pass on all four kill criteria produces a result the two PMs cannot explain to themselves or challenge on its own terms, so the finding cannot survive committee scrutiny no matter how rigorous the underlying work was.
issues.fix: Pair the sophisticated panel test (useful for killing the idea cheaply and correctly) with a simple, hand-checkable corroboration built for the audience: e.g., a small sample of the firm's own past 15-20 holdings, tone flagged plainly as improving/deteriorating quarter over quarter, checked by eye against what subsequently happened to the business.

issues.summary: The pass/fail gate is calibrated to systematic-strategy profitability (net spread ≥3% annualised, IR ≥0.4 on a monthly-rebalanced decile long-short) - a strategy this firm will never trade - so the kill criterion can discard a modest, real, single-name-relevant signal for failing an irrelevant tradability bar, or push the firm toward infrastructure spend it cannot use on a pass.
issues.why_it_applies_here: A spread/IR hurdle sized for a diversified quant sleeve has no natural translation to a 25-30 name concentrated book; the plan asserts it as the economic bar without ever asking what magnitude of tone signal would actually move conviction on one holding, so the number anchors the accept/reject decision to a P&L structure the firm does not run.
issues.what_breaks: The day-10 kill/pass decision and the day 11-14 branch: a 'kill' on IR<0.4 could bury a genuinely useful diligence signal, and a 'pass' commits to infrastructure or vendor licensing decisions the firm cannot operationalize.
issues.fix: Replace the systematic profitability gate with a decision-relevant threshold - e.g., does tone materially and consistently improve the hit rate or timing of the firm's own historical buy/trim decisions on the names it actually covers - and treat the Russell-3000 spread/IR figures as a secondary crowding check, not the primary bar.

issues.summary: The design never uses the evidence source most relevant to this firm - its own portfolio's historical earnings calls - relying instead entirely on Russell-3000 breadth.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The firm holds concentrated positions for years and presumably has a decade-plus of its own call transcripts and outcomes on file; per the stated preference for a firm's own record over a cross-sectional base rate when that record exists, this specific evidence was available and unused, in favor of a much harder-to-defend broad panel.
issues.what_breaks: Even a successful broad-panel result leaves unanswered whether tone would have flagged anything on the specific businesses this firm actually owned, which is the only question the IC will actually ask.
issues.fix: Run a cheap first pass on the firm's own 20-30 historical holdings' calls before or alongside the Russell-3000 build; if tone tracked known outcomes there, that is far more persuasive to this IC than a decile t-stat.

result.overall: The research design itself is unusually disciplined - pre-registration, a stated decay prior, vendor-crowding checks, four hard kill criteria, placebo and shuffle tests, and an explicit falsifier - and would be a credible piece of work for a systematic shop deciding whether to build or license a sentiment factor. But it is the wrong plan for this reader: it requires database infrastructure and statistical machinery this five-person concentrated long-only firm cannot build, run, or defend to its own IC, and even a clean pass produces a decile long-short factor product that has no place in a 25-30 name, three-to-five-year book. The fix is not more rigor, it is re-scoping the whole exercise around the firm's own holdings and a bar of proof the analyst and IC can actually inspect.

result.plan_implied_asker: a systematic/quant multi-strategy fund with tick-data infrastructure, engineering support, and a diversified, continuously-turned-over short-horizon trading book
result.what_would_falsify: If RLOIB's incremental Fama-MacBeth coefficient (controlling for ALLOIB and RETOIB) has |t|<2.0 at every horizon, the lot filter adds nothing; if it survives that but net-of-cost long-short alpha has t<2.0 under base costs, the effect is real but unharvestable. A stated falsifier exists and is not the problem here.

issues.summary: The entire pipeline requires infrastructure (WRDS/TAQ tick ingestion, Holden-Jacobsen trade cleaning, Lee-Ready/EMO/CLNV signing, Fama-MacBeth with Newey-West/Hansen-Hodrick/bootstrap SEs, square-root impact calibration, five paid vendor feeds) that this five-person shop with no engineers, no data scientists and no maintained database cannot build or run.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The brief states explicitly: Bloomberg, Excel, filings only, no engineers or data scientists, nobody maintains a database, and data is bought occasionally, not operated as infrastructure. This plan requires a continuously running multi-vendor quant pipeline, not a one-off purchase.
issues.what_breaks: The 'Data' and 'Methodology' steps cannot be executed at all with the stated tooling, so nothing downstream (predictive regressions, portfolios, evaluation) can ever be produced by this team.
issues.fix: Either fully outsource the build to a vendor/consultant who delivers a finished, auditable signal, or substitute a purchased retail-flow signal instead of constructing one from raw TAQ, or abandon the question as unanswerable in-house.

issues.summary: The tradeable deliverable is a daily-rebalanced, decile-sorted, dollar/beta-neutral long-short book with 5-day overlapping holds across hundreds of names — a different product than anything a 25-30 position, 3-5 year holding-period process can run.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The firm's stated edge is concentrated fundamental judgment held for years; even a statistically real RLOIB effect decays inside 20 trading days and demands a separate, continuously-turned-over sleeve with its own risk framework and dealing capability the firm does not have.
issues.what_breaks: The 'Portfolios' and 'Evaluation' steps produce an output (a systematic long-short book) the firm has no operational path to hold or act on, regardless of how strong the statistics are.
issues.fix: Reframe before starting: either narrow the question to whether the signal informs entry/exit timing on names already in the concentrated book, or recognize the deliverable is unusable and kill the project up front.

issues.summary: The statistical machinery (multi-estimator Fama-MacBeth SEs, competing signing algorithms, calibrated impact model) cannot be independently verified or defended by the analyst or the IC, and no simple hand-checkable corroboration is offered alongside it.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The mandate says the IC is skeptical of models it cannot inspect. This plan's conclusion turns on choices (which signing algorithm, which SE correction, which impact exponent) only a trained quant can evaluate, and the plan offers no plain, traceable check an IC member could redo by hand.
issues.what_breaks: The 'Evaluation' step's net-alpha t>3.0 verdict will be accepted or rejected on faith rather than on the merits, since the IC cannot interrogate any of the intermediate machinery.
issues.fix: Add a hand-auditable companion check (e.g., trace ten specific high-retail stock-days end to end from raw tape to computed imbalance) the analyst can walk the IC through, and drop the multi-estimator SE horse race in favor of one transparent method.

issues.summary: The plan never addresses whether retail-order-imbalance reversal is already a known, published, and commercially sold signal, or who on the other side is not simply already faster and better-resourced.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Off-exchange/round-lot retail-flow-based short-horizon reversal is an actively studied academic area with commercial data products already sold to market makers and quant funds; without engaging that, a passing result confirms a known, likely-crowded effect rather than an incremental finding.
issues.what_breaks: The 'Hypothesis' and 'Evaluation' steps present a passing net-alpha test as a discovery, but without a crowding/consensus check it may just be re-finding a picked-over effect this firm has no speed advantage to capture.
issues.fix: Before building the pipeline, survey what is already known and commercially sold about retail-imbalance signals and assess whether this firm's execution speed/cost structure could ever realize the edge even if the effect is real.

issues.summary: No cheap pilot is run before committing to full multi-vendor data licensing (TAQ, IHS Markit/Ortex, Thomson/Refinitiv 13F) and the entire cleaning/signing pipeline.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan's own falsification test (incremental Fama-MacBeth |t|<2.0) only needs TAQ+CRSP and a modest sample to get a first read, yet the plan licenses the full multi-year, multi-vendor dataset and builds the whole methodology stack before that first read is possible.
issues.what_breaks: By the time the 'Falsification' step actually runs, all data and vendor spend under 'Data' and 'Methodology' is already sunk.
issues.fix: Run the incremental regression on a one-year, few-hundred-name pilot with TAQ+CRSP only; license lending-fee and 13F data only if that pilot clears the bar.

issues.summary: The capacity analysis (net alpha across $50M-$5B AUM) answers a scaling question nobody asked for a $400M concentrated fund that would never run this as a stand-alone scalable sleeve.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The research question is binary (does the proxy identify profitable-to-fade retail flow); the firm's real constraint is its 3-5 year concentrated book, not the AUM scalability of a separate quant sleeve it has no vehicle to run.
issues.what_breaks: The 'Capacity' step produces a number that will be quoted as a real business opportunity when the firm cannot operationally deploy the sleeve at any AUM level.
issues.fix: Drop the capacity curve, or replace it with an explicit statement that it is out of scope given the firm has no vehicle to deploy such a strategy.

result.overall: This is a competently designed piece of academic-grade microstructure research, but it is the wrong plan for the asker on every axis that matters: the infrastructure it requires (TAQ tick pipelines, multi-vendor merges, Fama-MacBeth/Lee-Ready machinery) cannot be built or maintained by a five-person shop with no engineers or database, the deliverable (a daily-rebalanced cross-sectional long-short book) is incompatible with a 25-30 name, 3-5 year concentrated process, and the statistical apparatus is not something this IC can inspect or defend. It also never engages whether retail-imbalance reversal is already a crowded, commercially sold signal. The question could be answered far more cheaply by first asking whether this firm should ever operate this kind of strategy at all — that verdict is 'no,' and it does not require running any of the analysis to reach it.

result.plan_implied_asker: a systematic/quant trading desk with market-microstructure research capability, data engineering staff, and short-horizon liquidity-provision execution infrastructure
result.what_would_falsify: H0 is explicit and operationalized: round lots are an institutional VWAP/TWAP slicing artifact rather than a retail signature. The plan commits to reject H1 if lift <2.0x (or bootstrap lower bound <1.5x), recall <35%, signing accuracy <70% (hard stop <60%), stock-day correlation with Benchmark A <0.40 or Benchmark D <0.25, or panel regression |t|<3 — with the price-elasticity mechanism test (negative slope for RLP-flagged retail, flat for schedulers) as an independent discriminator.

issues.summary: The entire pipeline requires infrastructure and personnel (nanosecond TAQ, partitioned Parquet, DuckDB/Spark, exchange proprietary RLP feeds, Hui-Walter latent-class estimation) that a five-person shop with no engineers, no data scientists, and no maintained database cannot build, run, or keep current.
issues.why_it_applies_here: This specific plan spec's a permanent data-engineering stack (partitioned Parquet on DuckDB/Spark, continuously licensed exchange proprietary feeds, nanosecond TAQ ingestion) — not a one-off Excel analysis — against a firm whose stated tooling is Bloomberg, Excel and filings and which explicitly cannot operate infrastructure.
issues.what_breaks: The Data and Method sections cannot be executed by the one analyst the mandate specifies; if outsourced, the firm has purchased a black box, which contradicts the requirement that work be executable in-house and defensible to an IC that inspects what it approves.
issues.fix: Either drop the question as off-mandate, or replace it with a vendor-delivered, pre-computed retail-flow classification (a purchased dataset/report) that the analyst can read and sanity-check rather than build.

issues.summary: Even a fully successful result describes a short-horizon liquidity-provision/market-making strategy (Phase 2 go/no-go on after-cost Sharpe, spread decomposition, decile sorts) that this 3-5 year concentrated holder has no capital, mandate, or execution capability to run.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The firm's stated risk is being wrong about a business, not transaction costs, and it holds 25-30 names for years; the plan's own Phase 2 criteria (after-cost Sharpe ≥1.0, no negative year, net/gross >0.40) describe a market-making book operating on an intraday-to-days horizon that is structurally unrelated to how this firm makes or loses money.
issues.what_breaks: 36 months of specialized data licensing and analyst time are spent before anyone asks whether the firm could ever deploy the resulting signal; a positive Phase 1+2 result is unusable output.
issues.fix: Before any data purchase, get an explicit IC answer on whether the firm would ever underwrite a short-horizon liquidity-provision sleeve; if not, kill the project now rather than after the science is done.

issues.summary: The plan never argues why an outside party reconstructing retail flow from public TAQ/round-lot heuristics would retain an edge over the wholesalers who already know with certainty which orders are retail and already internalize/monetize that flow via PFOF.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan's own Benchmark B and C sources (RLP-certified market makers and Rule 605 wholesalers — Citadel Securities, Virtu, Two Sigma, Jane Street) are the exact counterparties with perfect, non-proxy knowledge of retail origination and first claim on the spread; a noisy round-lot proxy competes against agents who need no proxy at all.
issues.what_breaks: If Phase 2 finds a positive signal, there is no argument for why it survives contact with the wholesalers who already capture the retail spread before the flow ever reaches lit venues; the economics are asserted, not diffed against the informed counterparty.
issues.fix: Before building any signal, size how much of the retail-related spread is already captured by wholesaler internalization/PFOF and characterize only the residual, if any, as addressable.

issues.summary: The statistical machinery used even in Phase 1 alone (Hui-Walter latent-class precision estimation, Lee-Ready signing, double-clustered SE panel regressions, Benjamini-Hochberg correction) is not something one analyst can run or an IC skeptical of uninspectable models can evaluate.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The mandate explicitly states the IC is skeptical of models it cannot inspect and that the firm has no data scientists; latent-class label-noise models and clustered-SE panel regressions are not things this team can independently verify or defend in an IC meeting.
issues.what_breaks: The 'well-evidenced negative result' the plan promises as a deliverable cannot actually be delivered in a form the audience can check, so the conclusion has to be taken on faith from whoever built the pipeline.
issues.fix: Cut the deliverable down to what the plan itself already flags as sufficient and simple — Rule 605 wholesaler reports vs. FINRA OTC transparency by MPID, spreadsheet-only — and only escalate to TAQ/latent-class machinery if that simple check is genuinely ambiguous.

issues.summary: The plan states Rule 605 (Benchmark C) should run first because it alone can kill the project, but the Data/Method sections commit to full nanosecond TAQ ingestion and DuckDB/Spark infrastructure as part of the baseline design rather than strictly gating that spend behind C's outcome.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan itself identifies C as cheap and capable of killing the project alone, which means the expensive TAQ/RLP-feed/infrastructure spend described in the Data section is exactly the cost a genuinely sequential design would defer until after C fails to kill it.
issues.what_breaks: Infrastructure and licensing costs risk being committed in parallel with, rather than strictly after, the cheap test that could have ended the project for a fraction of the cost.
issues.fix: Make the plan explicitly conditional: run and report Benchmark C first as a standalone deliverable, and only provision TAQ/DuckDB/Spark infrastructure if C does not kill the hypothesis.

result.overall: As a piece of market-microstructure research the design is genuinely careful — it separates the identification claim from the trading claim, states a real alternative hypothesis (H0: round lots are an institutional slicing signature) with pre-committed kill thresholds, and triangulates noisy labels honestly. But it is written for a systematic desk with data engineering capability, not for a five-person concentrated long-only shop with no engineers, no database, and no interest in transaction costs; even a clean positive result would hand the firm a short-horizon liquidity-provision strategy it cannot execute, built on machinery its own IC cannot inspect, competing against wholesalers who already have the retail-identification problem solved with certainty. This should be killed at conception on firm-fit and edge grounds, not after 36 months of TAQ analysis.

result.plan_implied_asker: A concentrated fundamental/event-driven equity research shop with a multi-quarter-to-multi-year holding horizon and deep analyst bandwidth, for whom being wrong about the business is the risk that matters.
result.what_would_falsify: Negative on any of: negative implied gross bookings two straight quarters; channel inventory >1.5x normal; a backlog/LTA definition change in a quarter that would otherwise have declined; supplier finished-goods inventory rising two quarters while backlog is called record.

issues.summary: The plan is a bespoke, multi-quarter single-company forensic monograph built for a discretionary fundamental shop, not for a systematic firm judged on cost-surviving, capacity-bearing, non-crowded signals.
issues.why_it_applies_here: This firm's stated success criteria are transaction-cost survival, capacity, and crowding across a systematic book at days-to-weeks horizon; the plan instead produces a single qualitative verdict on one company's revenue durability with no stated mechanism for converting that into a sized, tradeable, replicable position, let alone a cross-sectional signal the 200-researcher platform would run across the universe.
issues.what_breaks: Downstream, even a correct fundamental conclusion has no defined path to a trade the desk can size, hedge, and monitor at its actual horizon.
issues.fix: Reframe as a screen: define the shortage-guidance event generically, specify what is measured cheaply and repeatably across many names (RPO delta, LTA announcement flag), and show how the single-name forensic depth here would generalize into an automatable cross-sectional feature.

issues.summary: The evidentiary horizon (multi-year LTAs, 8-quarter RPO bridges, 10-15 year capex schedules) is structurally mismatched to a days-to-weeks trading horizon.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The mechanism being tested (does shortage guidance convert into durable multi-year committed revenue) only resolves over multiple years by construction of the data used (LTA terms, capex depreciation schedules), while the firm trades and re-underwrites positions in days to weeks; nothing in the plan states when, within that multi-year resolution window, a days-to-weeks entry/exit is supposed to happen or why the market wouldn't have re-priced the name many times before resolution.
issues.what_breaks: Even a fully validated fundamental thesis leaves the trading desk with no answer to when to enter/exit or how to hold a multi-year fundamental view inside a days-to-weeks risk process.
issues.fix: State explicitly which shorter-horizon, higher-frequency proxy (e.g., reaction at guidance date, subsequent print drift) the desk would actually trade, and validate that proxy's timing separately from the multi-year durability claim.

issues.summary: Tier haircuts (90–95% / 70% / 25–35%) and the conjunctive threshold rule are calibrated mainly off one prior episode (2021–23 semiconductors) plus a handful of structurally different historical analogs, manufacturing false numeric precision.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Memory/passives 2017-18, semiconductors 2021-22, the current AI cycle, and telecom 2000 span different demand drivers, capital structures, and macro regimes; pooling four heterogeneous episodes to fix haircuts to the percentage point, then requiring six-plus of those calibrated thresholds to hold simultaneously, extracts more precision than a sample of this size and heterogeneity can support.
issues.what_breaks: The constructive/negative call becomes sensitive to which historical episode dominated the calibration, and the committee has no way to tell if the specific percentages are signal or artifact of the one best-documented episode (semiconductors).
issues.fix: Report haircuts as ranges derived per-episode rather than a single point estimate, and show how the constructive/negative call would flip under each episode's own calibration before treating the pooled number as ground truth.
