issues.summary: The cheapest test that could kill the idea — a quick historical look at how often shortage guidance in the four cited episodes actually preceded verified LTA growth — is buried at the end under Validation, after the full RPO bridge, agreement register, and DCF are already built.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan's own prior states enforceable, cash-backed commitment is usually weak, meaning the base rate of shortage guidance converting to durable revenue may simply be low; that base rate is checkable from the same four historical episodes cited later in Validation, cheaply, before committing to the company-specific forensic build.
issues.what_breaks: If the base-rate check would show the effect is rare or already fully priced by the time guidance is given, the entire agreement-register/tiering/DCF construction is sunk cost for nothing.
issues.fix: Run the four-episode historical base-rate check first as a standalone gate; only proceed to the full single-company bridge if it shows the effect is real and not already arbitraged away by the time of guidance.

issues.summary: The six-attribute scoring and tier assignment require sustained subjective judgment calls (e.g., what counts as 'real' take-or-pay, adversarial transcript reading) that are not mechanically reproducible by an independent researcher.
issues.why_it_applies_here: This firm's process explicitly depends on a research platform that replicates any result before it trades; a method whose core output depends on analyst judgment calls at each tiering step cannot be independently rerun to the same numbers, which is the specific verification workflow this firm relies on rather than a generic complaint about subjectivity.
issues.what_breaks: The research committee cannot re-derive the coverage percentages or the constructive/negative call without re-litigating every judgment call, defeating the stated replication step before deployment.
issues.fix: Convert the scoring rubric into a documented, deterministic decision tree with explicit rules per disclosure phrase, so two analysts working independently from the same filings produce the same tier assignments.

result.overall: This is careful, well-instrumented fundamental research — the falsifier is explicit, the reflexivity and enforcement caveats show real engagement with the other side, and the proxy-to-target validation via historical conversion rates is the right instinct. But it is built for the wrong shop: a systematic, days-to-weeks trading firm judged on cost-survival, capacity and crowding gets a multi-year, single-name, judgment-heavy monograph with no stated path to a tradeable, replicable, cross-sectional signal. The historical base-rate check buried in Validation should run first and could kill or greenlight the idea in a fraction of the proposed effort.

result.plan_implied_asker: A fundamental/event-driven desk building a cross-industry mechanism thesis to re-rate one company's multiple around a supply-shortage/LTA narrative, reasoning in fundamental quarters-to-years terms rather than a systematic book's cost/capacity/crowding scorecard
result.what_would_falsify: Episodes where contracted price stays materially above spot for 8+ quarters post-normalization, absent a hard qualification moat; for the live HBM case, failure of the pre-registered 3-5 checks (contract-liability direction, RPO growth threshold, customs tracking, obligation-table growth) within 12 months.

issues.summary: The plan never states how a mechanism that resolves over 4-12+ quarters converts into a position sized and held on the firm's stated days-to-weeks trading cadence.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The firm's edge and infrastructure are built around days-to-weeks turnover, but every outcome variable here (price/volume coding at T+4/8/12 quarters, HBM checks 'within 12 months') is a multi-quarter fundamental resolution; nothing in the plan says whether the trade is entered once and held for years or re-entered around each quarterly disclosure as a catalyst.
issues.what_breaks: At the trading-desk handoff, the research committee gets a haircut estimate with no mapping to entry/exit cadence, position duration, or which disclosure dates are the actual triggers, so the signal cannot be scheduled into the book without an ad hoc translation step.
issues.fix: Add an explicit step defining the tradeable event calendar (which quarterly disclosures are the informative catalysts) and state whether the position is a multi-quarter hold or a series of days-to-weeks trades around each print.

issues.why_it_applies_here: The brief explicitly states 'work is judged on whether a signal survives transaction costs, has capacity, and is not already crowded,' yet the deliverable stops at a probability-weighted haircut and a qualitative multiple statement with no mention of how many tradeable instances this event type produces per year, expected position size, or whether specialist commodity/semiconductor analysts already price the qualification-lag heuristic into their coverage.
issues.what_breaks: Even a fully validated mechanism produces no answer to whether this is investable at scale for this firm versus a one-off idiosyncratic override, which is exactly the question the committee will ask first.
issues.fix: Add a final stage, contingent on the mechanism holding, that counts historical frequency of qualifying guidance events per year across coverage, estimates realistic position count/size, and checks whether specialist coverage already reflects the qualification-lag distinction (crowding proxy).

issues.summary: Expensive data (PACER legal filings, customs/bill-of-lading records, full contract coding) is committed across all 20-30 episodes as a single block rather than triaged.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Several of the headline episodes (polysilicon vs. spot collapse, containers abandoned within months, aerospace/LNG holding) are visible in public price series alone; the bimodal split the hypothesis predicts should already be checkable on 4-5 of the most documented cases before paying for PACER litigation records and customs shipment data across the full 20-30 episode set.
issues.what_breaks: If the basic price-vs-spot divergence pattern fails to appear even in the clearest cases, the full contract-coding and legal-filing effort across the remaining episodes is sunk before that is known.
issues.fix: Run a cheap first pass on 4-5 highest-conviction episodes using only public price series and known contract type (take-or-pay vs. reservation) to confirm the bimodal split exists at all, before committing to full contract coding, PACER search, and customs data for the entire episode set.

issues.summary: The framework builds a general switching-cost taxonomy but never closes the loop by classifying the actual triggering company into that taxonomy.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The question as posed is about one company's guidance; the plan's deliverable is a general probability-weighted haircut framework and a statement of 'what would justify the higher multiple,' but nowhere does it commit to placing the specific company's industry and qualification lag on the aerospace-to-container spectrum to produce an actual call on that name.
issues.what_breaks: The committee receives a validated general mechanism but not an answer to the question that was asked, requiring an unstated final translation step that could itself be done carelessly under time pressure.
issues.fix: Add an explicit final step: classify the triggering company's product against the qualification-lag/switching-cost taxonomy built from the episode set, and state the resulting bucket-conditional base rate as the answer.

result.overall: This is a well-constructed mechanism test: it states a falsifiable hypothesis, builds negative controls (aerospace/LNG expected to hold, MLCC/containers expected to break) into the design rather than after the fact, pre-registers holdout and live-case checks, and uses rank-based base rates appropriate to a 20-30 episode N instead of a spurious regression. Its real gaps are practical rather than statistical: it never reconnects the general framework to the firm's stated judgment criteria (transaction costs, capacity, crowding) or trading horizon, and it front-loads expensive legal/customs data collection across the full episode set before a cheap price-series check on the clearest cases could confirm the pattern is there at all. Fixing the sequencing and adding the cost/capacity/crowding and company-classification steps would make this fully fit for purpose; as written it is a strong research design without a finished bridge to a trade.
